meta.blurb: One word, written in blood, is all the dead man leaves behind on the wall. A stranger named Sherlock Holmes reads the empty house like a book, and his new friend Dr Watson learns how far back a murder can reach.
meta.bible: Sherlock Holmes: the consulting detective of Baker Street, tall, lean, sharp-eyed, proud of his method. Dr John Watson: an army doctor wounded in Afghanistan, Holmes's new friend and the narrator. Stamford: the old friend who introduces them. Mrs Hudson: their landlady at 221B Baker Street. Gregson and Lestrade: two Scotland Yard detectives, proud and often wrong. Enoch Drebber: the dead man, from Cleveland, Ohio. Joseph Stangerson: his secretary, also killed. Mrs Charpentier, Alice and Arthur Charpentier: the family with whom Drebber lodged. Constable Rance: the policeman who saw a drunk man at the gate. Wiggins: leader of the Baker Street Irregulars, street boys who help Holmes. Jefferson Hope: a cab driver, the murderer, a hunter from America. John Ferrier: an American who is saved in the desert. Lucy Ferrier: the little girl he saves and adopts; Hope's love. Utah, Salt Lake City: where the second part happens, 1847 and after. The elders: the leaders of the settlers' community; the story is a Victorian novel's picture and not a fair picture of any real people. 221B Baker Street, Lauriston Gardens, Brixton Road, Criterion Bar, St Bartholomew's hospital, Scotland Yard, Afghanistan, Maiwand, London, Cleveland, Ohio. Rache: the German word for revenge, written in blood. Voice and tone: clear, clever and steady, a puzzle solved step by step; deaths are stated plainly without gore; the second half is sorrowful, then calm. Added for the full-length book: Netley: the army medical school where Watson trained. Peshawar: the base hospital in India where Watson lay ill with fever. Murray: Watson's orderly, who carried him to safety. Orontes: the troopship that brought Watson home to Portsmouth. Portsmouth, the Strand, Holborn: places in England. Bart's: St Bartholomew's hospital, where Holmes works in the laboratory. Marines: the sergeant who brings the note is a retired Marine. Hallé's concert: where Holmes hears Norman Neruda play the violin. Cremona: the town of the great violins; Stradivarius made them. Trichinopoly: the kind of cigar whose ash Holmes finds. Audley Court, Kennington Lane: where Constable Rance lives. Murcher: the second constable who helped hold the drunk man. Sally and Duncan Street, Houndsditch: the false story told by the old woman. Torquay Terrace, Camberwell: where Madame Charpentier keeps her boarding house. Euston: the railway station. Halliday's Private Hotel: where Stangerson is killed. Daily News, Standard, Telegraph: London newspapers. Jefferson Hope's story is told in the second part: the Great Alkali Plain, Missouri, Nevada, the Sierra Nevada mountains, Eagle Canyon, the Wasatch mountains, the Mormons or Saints, Brigham Young the Prophet, the Danites or Avenging Angels, Elder Stangerson and Elder Drebber (the fathers of the two young men), Kemball, Cowper, Sacramento, Washington, St Petersburg, Copenhagen, Paris, Liverpool, the Guion Steamship Company. The time of the main story is 1881; Hope's story begins in 1847 and the flight is in 1860. Hope is dying of an aneurysm.
chapters: The Man Who Beats the Dead
An Empty House in Brixton Road

beats.scene: A young army doctor in uniform boards a ship bound for India
beats.summary: John Watson takes his medical degree, trains as an army surgeon and is sent to India as war breaks out in Afghanistan.

beats.scene: A soldier is carried across a pack-horse away from the battle at Maiwand
beats.summary: At the battle of Maiwand a bullet shatters Watson's shoulder, and his orderly Murray carries him to safety.

beats.scene: A feverish patient lies in a crowded hospital ward at Peshawar
beats.summary: Watson recovers a little at Peshawar, then falls ill with fever and is close to death for months.

beats.scene: A thin, pale man steps off a troopship onto the quay at Portsmouth
beats.summary: Watson is sent home on the Orontes with his health ruined and nine months' leave to recover.

beats.scene: A lonely man walks the crowded pavements of London with a small bag
beats.summary: With no family and only a small army pension, Watson drifts to London, where idle people from all over the Empire end up.

beats.scene: A man sits alone in a dreary hotel room on the Strand
beats.summary: Watson takes a room in a dull hotel and spends his money more freely than he should.

beats.scene: A man counts coins on a bed beside an open account book
beats.summary: Watson sees that his money is running out and decides to leave the hotel for cheaper rooms.

beats.scene: A young man taps a thin stranger on the shoulder in a busy bar
beats.summary: On the very day he decides, Watson is tapped on the shoulder in the Criterion Bar by his old friend Stamford.

beats.scene: Two old friends eat lunch at a table in a Holborn restaurant
beats.summary: Stamford is shocked at how thin and brown Watson looks, and Watson tells him his story over lunch.

beats.scene: Watson leans across a restaurant table, listening to his friend with surprise
beats.summary: When Watson says he needs rooms to share, Stamford says he is the second person to say so that day.

beats.scene: Stamford speaks quietly across a lunch table, one hand raised in warning
beats.summary: Stamford warns that Sherlock Holmes is queer in his ideas and an enthusiast, though a decent fellow.

beats.scene: Shelves of strange books and bottles in a student's untidy room
beats.summary: Holmes is not a medical student but knows anatomy and chemistry, and his odd knowledge would astonish his professors.

beats.scene: A pale young man swings a stick at a body in a dissecting room
beats.summary: Stamford says he once saw Holmes beating bodies with a stick to learn how far bruises form after death.

beats.scene: A friend hesitates with a glass in one hand, looking uneasy
beats.summary: Stamford says Holmes is cold-blooded and might try a new poison on a friend, out of curiosity, then take it himself.

beats.scene: Two men walk up the steps of a large London hospital
beats.summary: Stamford leads Watson to the hospital but warns that he will not answer for what happens if they quarrel.

beats.scene: A tall thin man bends over a test tube in a bare laboratory
beats.summary: In the laboratory Holmes cries out that he has found a test that detects blood.

beats.scene: A scientist holds up a glass tube full of dull brown water
beats.summary: Holmes explains how the new test shows blood in even the oldest stain, and why it would matter in a court of law.

beats.scene: A man pricks his finger and drops blood into a jar of water
beats.summary: Holmes pricks his finger and shows the test: a few drops of blood turn a jar of clear water brown.

beats.scene: A cheerful thin stranger shakes hands with a startled army doctor
beats.summary: Holmes is introduced to Watson and says at once that he has been in Afghanistan.

beats.scene: Two men talk by a bench and agree on a plan, shaking hands
beats.summary: Holmes and Watson confess their bad habits to one another and agree to look at rooms in Baker Street the next day.

beats.scene: Two men look round a bright sitting room with two wide windows
beats.summary: Holmes and Watson inspect the rooms at 221B Baker Street, find them perfect and take them that same day.

beats.scene: A landlady in a white cap welcomes two men carrying boxes upstairs
beats.summary: Watson moves in that evening and Holmes follows next morning with many boxes; Mrs Hudson, the landlady, settles them in.

beats.scene: A tall man puts on his hat and leaves a quiet house early
beats.summary: Holmes lives a quiet, regular life, up early and out before Watson, working in the laboratory, the dissecting rooms or on long walks.

beats.scene: A thin man lies on a sofa with his eyes half closed
beats.summary: At times Holmes lies silent on the sofa for days, and Watson wonders about drugs but sees that his clean habits forbid the idea.

beats.scene: A lean man with a hawk-like nose studies a glass tube
beats.summary: Watson describes Holmes: over six feet tall, lean, sharp-eyed and hawk-nosed, with ink-stained hands and a delicate touch.

beats.scene: A man writes a numbered list in a notebook under a lamp
beats.summary: Watson writes a list of what Holmes knows: literature, philosophy and astronomy nothing, politics feeble.

beats.scene: A list in a notebook: chemistry, geology, violin, boxing, law
beats.summary: Holmes is deep in chemistry and geology, knows sensational crimes, and is a boxer, swordsman and violinist.

beats.scene: A man with a violin sits in a chair, eyes closed, playing softly
beats.summary: Holmes plays the violin well, sometimes sweetly, sometimes strangely, and Watson wonders what the man really is.

beats.scene: Two men over breakfast, one of them explaining on his fingers
beats.summary: Holmes explains how he guessed Afghanistan, and calls the detectives Dupin and Lecoq inferior to himself.

beats.scene: A shabby visitor and a young woman wait at a door on a landing
beats.summary: A stream of odd visitors comes to Holmes, and Watson learns from him that they are his clients.

beats.scene: Watson stares in surprise at Holmes beside a window and a book
beats.summary: Watson learns that Holmes does not know the earth goes round the sun, and Holmes explains that a brain is like a small attic.

beats.scene: A thin man taps his forehead beside a shelf full of tools
beats.summary: Holmes says a wise man stocks his attic only with tools useful to his work, and he would forget the sun at once.

beats.scene: A bored man at a breakfast table reads a magazine in a sunny window
beats.summary: On a dull morning Watson reads a magazine article called The Book of Life.

beats.scene: A magazine article describes a drop of water linked to a river
beats.summary: The article says a thinker could tell a whole chain from a single link, from a drop of water to an ocean.

beats.scene: A man throws a magazine on the table and laughs while Holmes watches
beats.summary: Watson calls the article twaddle, and Holmes quietly says that he wrote it himself.

beats.scene: Holmes sits in an armchair with his fingertips together, looking calm
beats.summary: Holmes says he is a consulting detective, the only one in the world, whom other detectives consult when they fail.

beats.scene: Holmes talks across the table about papers and an old crime book
beats.summary: Holmes says crimes resemble each other and his knowledge of past crimes helps him unravel new ones for private agencies.

beats.scene: Two men stand at a bay window looking down at a busy street
beats.summary: Watson doubts him, and Holmes points to a man in the street below and says he is a retired sergeant of Marines.

beats.scene: A broad man with a blue envelope looks up at a doorway
beats.summary: The man comes to the door with a letter, admits he was a sergeant of Marines, and Holmes explains how he knew.

beats.scene: Holmes tears open an envelope and reads quickly with a bright look
beats.summary: Holmes reads the letter from Gregson of Scotland Yard, asking for help with a murder.

beats.scene: Holmes holds a short letter up to the window light
beats.summary: Gregson's letter says a man named Enoch Drebber has been found dead in an empty house with no wound, and Holmes talks about Gregson and Lestrade.

beats.scene: Holmes sits back in his chair with his legs crossed, refusing to rise
beats.summary: Holmes says he is too lazy to go and that Gregson will take the credit, then at last he agrees to go.

beats.scene: Two men in a four-wheeled cab clatter along a London street
beats.summary: In the cab Holmes talks of violins and Cremona while Watson grows impatient, and Holmes says it is a mistake to guess before he has facts.

beats.scene: A cab stops outside a dull, dirty house in a quiet road
beats.summary: They reach Brixton Road and the empty house at number three, Lauriston Gardens, with a crowd of idlers at the gate.

beats.scene: A police inspector greets two men on a muddy garden path
beats.summary: Gregson greets them and Holmes comments on the path, trodden by so many feet that it looks as if a herd of buffaloes had passed.

beats.scene: Holmes kneels at the garden gate with a magnifying glass
beats.summary: Gregson boasts, and Holmes asks whether they came by cab, then studies the path, the gate and the road with his glass.

beats.scene: A bare room with peeling paper, thick dust and a red candle stump
beats.summary: The men enter the front room of the empty house, which is dusty, dirty and lit only by one hazy window.

beats.scene: A well-dressed man lies on his back on a dusty floor
beats.summary: The dead man lies on the floor, about forty-three, well dressed, with a face full of horror and hatred.

beats.scene: A police inspector lays a watch, cards and a book on a table
beats.summary: Gregson lists what was in the dead man's pockets: a gold watch, cards bearing the name Drebber, money and a book with Stangerson's name.

beats.scene: Holmes bends close to the dead man's lips and breathes in
beats.summary: Holmes examines the body closely, sniffs the lips, and learns that there is no wound, so the blood on the floor must belong to someone else.

beats.scene: A dark red word is written on a peeling wall in a bare room
beats.summary: On the wall in a corner is the word RACHE, written in blood, which Gregson points out.

beats.scene: A detective with a notebook points at the wall, looking very sure
beats.summary: Lestrade says it is the start of the name Rachel and the writer was interrupted, and both detectives look pleased.

beats.scene: Two men lift a body, and a gold ring rolls across the floor
beats.summary: When the body is moved, a woman's gold wedding ring rolls out on the floor, and Gregson takes it for a great clue.

beats.scene: Holmes crawls on the floor with a tape measure and a round glass
beats.summary: Holmes takes a tape and a magnifying glass and crawls over the floor, measuring and muttering.

beats.scene: Holmes scrapes grey ash from the floor into a small envelope
beats.summary: Holmes collects a little grey ash from the floor and studies the footprints in the dust.

beats.scene: Holmes measures the wall and the length of a stride on the floor
beats.summary: Holmes works out the killer's height from the length of his stride and from the height of the letters on the wall.

beats.scene: A fingernail has left four long scratches in the plaster beneath a word
beats.summary: Holmes sees the killer's square-toed boots and the long scratches made by his fingernail in the plaster.

beats.scene: A cab with a horse stands in a muddy road under grey light
beats.summary: Holmes says the killer came in a cab drawn by a horse with one new shoe, and that his face was red.

beats.scene: Two detectives exchange doubtful smiles beside the dead man
beats.summary: Gregson and Lestrade smile at his list but ask how the man was killed, and Holmes answers: poison.

beats.scene: Holmes turns back at the door with one finger raised
beats.summary: At the door Holmes tells them that Rache is German for revenge, and that they should not waste time looking for Miss Rachel.

beats.scene: Holmes and Watson walk side by side down a gloomy London street
beats.summary: Outside the house Watson asks how Holmes knows so much, and Holmes explains that the murderer's nose bled, which is why he thinks the man is red-faced.

beats.scene: Holmes points at cab wheel marks and horse prints in the road
beats.summary: Holmes explains how the wheel marks and hoof prints in the road told him of a cab and a horse with one new shoe.

beats.scene: Holmes talks while Watson listens, both walking in the early afternoon
beats.summary: Holmes says nothing was stolen, so the motive was revenge, and he thinks the word on the wall was meant to mislead the police.

beats.scene: Holmes writes a telegram at a post office counter
beats.summary: Holmes sends a telegram to the police in Cleveland, asking if Drebber had married and whether he had enemies.

beats.scene: A narrow lane with a row of small houses and an open door
beats.summary: Holmes and Watson find the house of Constable Rance in Audley Court, off Kennington Lane.

beats.scene: A policeman in shirt sleeves sits at a kitchen table, telling a story
beats.summary: Rance says he was on his beat at one in the morning and found the empty house with the door open and a light.

beats.scene: A drunk man leans against a gate, singing loudly at night
beats.summary: Rance says that after he found the body he came back to the gate and a drunk man was leaning there, singing.

beats.scene: A constable describes a tall man with a red face and a brown coat
beats.summary: Rance describes the drunk man as tall and red-faced with his chin muffled in a brown overcoat, and says he had no whip.

beats.scene: Holmes drops a coin on a table and shakes his head at a policeman
beats.summary: Holmes gives Rance half a sovereign and scolds him, because the man he held in his hands was the murderer.

beats.scene: Holmes stands in the street with his hat tilted, thinking
beats.summary: Holmes works out that the murderer went back for the ring and that the ring is the way to catch him.

beats.scene: Holmes writes at a desk while Watson waits with a hat in hand
beats.summary: Holmes writes an advertisement saying a gold wedding ring has been found in Brixton Road, and Watson takes it to the newspapers.

beats.scene: A printed notice in a newspaper column about a found gold ring
beats.summary: The notice gives Watson's name, not Holmes's, and asks the owner to call at Baker Street between eight and nine that evening.

beats.scene: A lady plays a violin on a bright concert stage before a large audience
beats.summary: While they wait, Holmes takes Watson to Hallé's concert to hear Norman Neruda play the violin, and he is gentle and dreamy.

beats.scene: Watson sits by a lamp holding a ring while Holmes reads a book
beats.summary: In the evening Watson waits in the sitting room with the ring while Holmes sits in the corner, ready to listen.

beats.scene: An old woman in a shawl stands in a dim doorway holding a stick
beats.summary: At nine o'clock a bent old woman is shown up by Mrs Hudson, saying she has come about the ring.

beats.scene: An old woman talks fast and shakes her stick near a lamp
beats.summary: The old woman says the ring belongs to her daughter Sally, who is married to a steward on a Union boat.

beats.scene: An old woman takes a small ring from Watson's hand and hurries off
beats.summary: Watson gives her the ring, and she thanks him quickly and hurries off down the stairs.

beats.scene: Holmes throws on his coat and runs down the dark stairs
beats.summary: As soon as the door shuts, Holmes puts on his coat and hat and follows her out into the street.

beats.scene: A man clings to the back of a cab speeding through gaslit streets
beats.summary: Holmes tells Watson later that he followed the woman, saw her take a cab and jumped on behind it.

beats.scene: Holmes opens an empty cab door in a quiet street and laughs at himself
beats.summary: At the end of the ride the cab was empty and no one of the name lived there, so Holmes admits he was beaten.

beats.scene: Newspapers lie spread across a breakfast table at Baker Street
beats.summary: The next morning every paper is full of the Brixton mystery, and the Standard says the crime was the work of foreign political refugees.

beats.scene: Holmes laughs over a newspaper beside a cup of coffee
beats.summary: Holmes laughs at the papers' wild theories, and says that whatever happens Gregson and Lestrade will have the credit.

beats.scene: A smiling police detective enters a sitting room and rubs his hands
beats.summary: Gregson arrives, delighted, and says he has made the whole matter as clear as day and has arrested a man.

beats.scene: A neat boarding house stands at the end of a quiet London terrace
beats.summary: Gregson says he went to Madame Charpentier's boarding house in Camberwell, where Drebber and Stangerson had lodged for three weeks.

beats.scene: A young woman with a worried face stands before a drunken lodger
beats.summary: Madame Charpentier's daughter Alice told how Drebber had insulted her, and her brother Arthur beat him out of the house.

beats.scene: A young naval officer returns late at night, carrying a heavy stick
beats.summary: Drebber left for the Liverpool train that evening, and Arthur came home after midnight and could not say where he had been.

beats.scene: A detective explains his theory to Holmes, who listens with a strange smile
beats.summary: Gregson says that Arthur followed Drebber and killed him, and Holmes politely congratulates him.

beats.scene: A pale detective bursts into the room, holding his hat in his hand
beats.summary: Lestrade rushes in white-faced to say that Stangerson was found murdered at Halliday's Private Hotel.

beats.scene: A porter on a dark hotel stairway points to a ladder against a window
beats.summary: Lestrade tells how Stangerson came home late, and how a milk-boy saw a man climbing down a ladder from his window.

beats.scene: A stabbed man lies in a hotel room beneath a word in blood
beats.summary: Stangerson lay stabbed in his room, and above him on the wall the same word RACHE was written in blood.

beats.scene: Holmes studies a stained wall in a small hotel bedroom
beats.summary: At the hotel Holmes finds that the second word on the wall matches the first and tells Lestrade that the same man killed both.

beats.scene: A small box with two round pills lies on a hotel washstand
beats.summary: A small box holding two pills is found in the room, and Holmes takes it away as a most important clue.

beats.scene: A kind landlady holds a trembling old terrier in her arms
beats.summary: At Baker Street Holmes asks to borrow Mrs Hudson's old, sick terrier, which Watson was about to put out of its pain.

beats.scene: A dog laps milk from a saucer on the sitting-room floor
beats.summary: Holmes cuts one pill in half, mixes it in milk and gives it to the terrier, and nothing happens.

beats.scene: A small dog lies still on a rug beside a saucer
beats.summary: Holmes tries the second pill in the same way, and the terrier falls dead in an instant.

beats.scene: Holmes holds up a small box between two fingers
beats.summary: Holmes explains that one pill was harmless and the other deadly, and the murderer made his victim choose.

beats.scene: A telegram on a tray beside a cup and a plate
beats.summary: A telegram arrives from Cleveland saying Drebber once asked for protection from a rival in love named Jefferson Hope, now in Europe.

beats.scene: A dozen ragged street boys crowd into a sitting room
beats.summary: Holmes calls in Wiggins and the street boys and sends them to find the cabman, and soon the cab is found.

beats.scene: A cabman bends over a trunk while two detectives stand behind him
beats.summary: Holmes asks the cabman to help with a trunk, and while the man bends over it, the handcuffs click on his wrists.

beats.scene: A strong man struggles, then sits still with a calm face
beats.summary: Jefferson Hope breaks a window in his struggle, then grows calm and says he is dying and wants to tell his story.

beats.scene: A vast, dry, grey plain stretches under a hot, cloudless sky
beats.summary: Hope begins his story with the Great Alkali Plain, a lifeless desert in the middle of America where nothing grows.

beats.scene: A gaunt man and a small girl sit beside a rock in the desert
beats.summary: In May 1847, a worn-out man named John Ferrier and a little girl of about five sit beside a rock in the desert.

beats.scene: A thin man looks at an empty water flask and a dead mule
beats.summary: Ferrier's mules have died, his water is gone, and the rest of his party has been lost to thirst and hardship.

beats.scene: A little girl looks up at the man and asks him a question
beats.summary: Lucy asks for her mother and father, and Ferrier tells her gently that they have gone away and he will look after her.

beats.scene: A man gives the last drop of water to a child from a flask
beats.summary: Ferrier gives his last mouthful of water to Lucy and keeps none for himself.

beats.scene: A girl sleeps in a man's arms while he looks toward the horizon
beats.summary: Lucy falls asleep in his arms, and Ferrier thinks they will die before the next morning.

beats.scene: A faint cloud of dust rises on the distant edge of a desert
beats.summary: Ferrier sees a small cloud of white dust far to the east and cannot tell what it is.

beats.scene: A long train of covered wagons rolls slowly across a dry plain
beats.summary: The cloud grows into a long train of covered wagons and many horsemen travelling toward the west.

beats.scene: A horseman gets down and gives a man water from a cup
beats.summary: A rider reaches Ferrier and Lucy, gives them water from his flask and carries them toward the wagons.

beats.scene: A stern old man in a plain coat looks down at a rescued man
beats.summary: An elder of the wagon train says they are Saints of the Prophet and will take Ferrier and Lucy if they accept his faith.

beats.scene: A weary man nods to a stern elder beside a covered wagon
beats.summary: Ferrier agrees to follow the elder's faith, and the elder says he and the child may ride in the wagons.

beats.scene: A kind woman wraps a sleeping child in a blanket inside a wagon
beats.summary: Lucy is cared for by a kind woman in the wagon, and Ferrier slowly gains back his strength.

beats.scene: A line of wagons crosses a wide, shallow river with oxen
beats.summary: The wagon train struggles on for weeks across rivers and mountains, and the Saints work hard together.

beats.scene: A man rides ahead of a wagon train with a rifle on his shoulder
beats.summary: Ferrier proves himself a fine hunter and guide, and the Saints begin to respect him.

beats.scene: A green valley opens before a long line of wagons, with a lake beyond
beats.summary: At last the train reaches a broad green valley beside a great salt lake, which their Prophet says is their new home.

beats.scene: A man in a dark coat marks out squares on the ground with sticks
beats.summary: The Prophet, Brigham Young, plans a city, and every family receives land according to his rank in the church.

beats.scene: A man builds a log house with an axe, with a child nearby
beats.summary: Ferrier is given a fine piece of land and builds a log house for himself and Lucy.

beats.scene: A farm with green fields, fat cattle and fruit trees in the sun
beats.summary: Ferrier works hard and is clever with land, and within a few years he is one of the richest farmers in the valley.

beats.scene: A rich man refuses a plate of food at a table of elders
beats.summary: The Saints often urge Ferrier to take wives, as they do, but he refuses, and his neighbours begin to whisper.

beats.scene: A small girl in a bright dress picks flowers at a farm gate
beats.summary: Lucy grows up healthy and cheerful on the farm, and Ferrier loves her as if she were his own daughter.

beats.scene: A smiling girl on a brown horse rides along a farm road at dawn
beats.summary: Thirteen years pass, and Lucy, nearly a woman, is known across the valley as the Flower of Utah.

beats.scene: A wide herd of wild cattle thunders down a dusty street
beats.summary: One day in May 1860 Lucy rides to town, and a great herd of cattle comes down the road toward her.

beats.scene: A girl's horse is trapped among horned cattle in a cloud of dust
beats.summary: Lucy's horse is caught in the middle of the herd, and she is in great danger of being trampled.

beats.scene: A young hunter on a horse pulls a girl from the path of cattle
beats.summary: A young stranger rides in, lifts Lucy to safety and leads her out through the herd.

beats.scene: A tall tanned man in a rough coat takes off his hat
beats.summary: The stranger says that his name is Jefferson Hope, a hunter who has come from the silver mines of Nevada.

beats.scene: A girl tells her father her story while a stranger waits
beats.summary: Lucy tells her father about the rescue, and Ferrier thanks Hope warmly and invites him to the farm.

beats.scene: A young man and a young woman sit on a porch under the stars
beats.summary: Hope stays at the farm for weeks, and he and Lucy walk together in the evening and fall deeply in love.

beats.scene: A young man speaks seriously to an older man by a fireplace
beats.summary: Hope asks Ferrier for Lucy's hand, and Ferrier is glad, but worried that the elders will not approve.

beats.scene: An old farmer holds a young man's hand firmly beside a gate
beats.summary: Ferrier agrees to the marriage, if Hope will go back to Nevada, earn enough money and return within two months.

beats.scene: A hunter on a horse rides away down a road while a girl waves
beats.summary: Hope promises to come back, and he rides away toward Nevada while Lucy waves from the gate.

beats.scene: A lonely girl sits on a porch step, gazing at an empty road
beats.summary: Weeks go by, and Lucy misses Hope badly, while Ferrier works and worries about the future.

beats.scene: A stern man on a horse rides up to a farm gate at dusk
beats.summary: One evening Brigham Young himself rides up to Ferrier's gate, and Ferrier, alarmed, welcomes him in.

beats.scene: A powerful man in a dark coat sits stiffly at a farmhouse table
beats.summary: The Prophet says that Ferrier has been well treated but has never truly joined the church.

beats.scene: A powerful man points to two young men's names on a paper
beats.summary: The Prophet says that Lucy is now grown and must marry the son of Elder Stangerson or the son of Elder Drebber.

beats.scene: An old farmer stands at his door with his head bowed and hands clasped
beats.summary: Ferrier asks for time, and the Prophet gives him thirty days and says that he must obey.

beats.scene: The Prophet rides away into the dark, and a man watches with fear
beats.summary: The Prophet leaves, and Ferrier is left in terror, for he knows that men who refuse the elders sometimes vanish.

beats.scene: A man at night looks at a map of mountain passes and a gun
beats.summary: Ferrier lies awake making plans, but he knows that the mountain passes are watched and that he cannot flee without Hope.

beats.scene: A father and daughter hold hands in a farmhouse kitchen
beats.summary: Ferrier tells Lucy what the Prophet has said, and she says she would die before she married either young man.

beats.scene: A man gives a folded letter to a rider in a field at dawn
beats.summary: Ferrier sends a secret message to Hope by a trusted traveller, begging him to come back at once.

beats.scene: Two proud young men stand in a doorway arguing with an old man
beats.summary: The two young suitors come to the farm, each insisting that Lucy must marry him, and Ferrier drives them out.

beats.scene: A worried man marks days on a calendar on a farmhouse wall
beats.summary: Ferrier counts the days of the Prophet's deadline and tells Lucy to keep her courage.

beats.scene: A paper with a number is pinned to a blanket
beats.summary: A few days into the thirty, Ferrier wakes to find a paper pinned to his blanket with the number twenty-six written on it.

beats.scene: A number is painted in white on a wooden gate in the early light
beats.summary: Each morning a new, smaller number appears, on the wall, on the gate or on the floor, and nobody sees who writes it.

beats.scene: A man stands alone in a field while neighbours turn their backs
beats.summary: The neighbours stop speaking to Ferrier, and the whole valley seems to watch him in silence.

beats.scene: A man sits at night by an open window, rifle across his knees
beats.summary: Ferrier sits up each night with a rifle, but nothing happens, and the numbers keep falling.

beats.scene: A girl cries at a kitchen table beside an unlit lamp
beats.summary: With three days left, Lucy weeps, for there is still no word from Hope.

beats.scene: A shadow taps at a dark window late at night
beats.summary: On the night before the second last day, there is a soft tapping at the window, and Ferrier takes up his rifle.

beats.scene: A young hunter in a dusty coat comes in at a low door
beats.summary: The stranger is Jefferson Hope, who has ridden hard from Nevada and has come in secret.

beats.scene: Hope spreads out a map on a table as two others lean over it
beats.summary: Hope says they must leave that same night, and he explains his plan for getting through the sentinels.

beats.scene: A man and a girl pack bags in a dark kitchen by candlelight
beats.summary: Ferrier and Lucy quickly pack food and water, and leave their house and their rich farm behind forever.

beats.scene: Three figures creep out of a dark farmyard toward a clump of trees
beats.summary: Ferrier, Lucy and Hope slip out at midnight and find the horses and a pack mule that Hope has hidden among the trees.

beats.scene: Three riders move in silence along a dark road beneath a pale moon
beats.summary: They ride all night without speaking, with Lucy wrapped in a blanket and Hope leading the way over the fields.

beats.scene: A guard with a rifle stands in a narrow mountain pass at night
beats.summary: At the first pass a sentinel challenges them from the dark, and Hope answers with the secret sign, and they are allowed through.

beats.scene: A second guard in the dim light lowers his gun and waves them on
beats.summary: At the second post Hope gives another sign, and the guard waves them on without a word.

beats.scene: The first grey light shows a steep rocky mountainside ahead
beats.summary: As dawn breaks, they leave the road and climb into the mountains, with the valley far behind them.

beats.scene: A narrow ledge winds along a cliff above a deep gorge
beats.summary: Hope leads them along a hidden track on a narrow ledge, and the horses have to be led carefully by hand.

beats.scene: Three people crouch behind rocks while riders pass on the road
beats.summary: At a third pass they hear riders approaching, and they hide in the rocks until the patrol has passed by.

beats.scene: A small hollow among tall rocks, with a tiny fire and blankets
beats.summary: By nightfall they reach a hidden hollow in Eagle Canyon, where they rest and eat the last of their food.

beats.scene: A tired man talks quietly to a young hunter beside a thin fire
beats.summary: Hope says they must have meat if they are to go on, and that he will hunt for it in the morning.

beats.scene: A hunter with a rifle climbs a mountain slope at dawn, waving back
beats.summary: At dawn Hope takes his rifle and climbs the mountain, promising to be back by evening.

beats.scene: A hunter climbs through a maze of rocky canyons with a rifle
beats.summary: Hope hunts all day without luck, then shoots a mountain sheep, and in the dusk he loses his way among the canyons.

beats.scene: A hunter with a sheep on his back calls into a dark empty hollow
beats.summary: Hope reaches the hollow late at night, but there is no fire, no sound and no answer when he calls.

beats.scene: A hunter finds scattered blankets and the marks of many horses
beats.summary: He finds the camp torn up, with the marks of many horses and a new mound of earth beside the spring.

beats.scene: A rough wooden marker stands on a fresh grave in a canyon
beats.summary: On the grave is a paper stating that John Ferrier has died, and there is no sign of Lucy.

beats.scene: A young man kneels by a grave with his head in his hands
beats.summary: Hope kneels in despair, and then, filled with anger, he decides to follow the men who took Lucy.

beats.scene: A hunter hides in the shade as two men meet beside a barn
beats.summary: Hope creeps back toward the valley and meets Cowper, an old friend among the Saints, who hides him.

beats.scene: An old farmer whispers a sad story to a young man at night
beats.summary: Cowper tells him how the elders' men found the Ferriers, killed Ferrier and carried Lucy back to the town.

beats.scene: A pale girl is led before a stern, proud young man
beats.summary: Lucy is forced to marry Drebber, who takes over her father's farm and cattle.

beats.scene: A pale girl sits by a window as her face grows thin and sad
beats.summary: Lucy fades under her grief, and within a month she is dead.

beats.scene: A young hunter bends over a still, pale girl in candlelight
beats.summary: Hope slips into the house at night, kisses her forehead and takes the wedding ring from her finger, vowing revenge.

beats.scene: A young man slips out of a dark house and runs into the hills
beats.summary: After taking the ring, Hope nearly meets a guard, but he escapes and hides in the mountains for many weeks.

beats.scene: A bearded man in a ragged hat looks at an empty house and farm
beats.summary: A year later Hope returns in disguise and learns that Drebber and Stangerson have quarrelled with the church and left Utah.

beats.scene: A lone traveller walks beside a railway line toward a distant city
beats.summary: Hope follows their trail across America, working in mines and on farms when he needs money.

beats.scene: A man peers into a crowded city street from a doorway
beats.summary: For years he searches town after town, always carrying the wedding ring, and always a little behind them.

beats.scene: Hope sees Drebber across a busy street in a large American city
beats.summary: At last in Cleveland, Hope sees Drebber in the street, but Drebber also sees him and runs.

beats.scene: A judge at a high desk looks sternly at a ragged young man
beats.summary: Drebber asks the law for protection, and Hope is brought before a judge who sends him to jail for a time.

beats.scene: A ship sails away from a grey American harbour at dawn
beats.summary: When Hope is freed, he finds that Drebber and Stangerson have taken all their money and fled to Europe.

beats.scene: A poor traveller scrubs a ship's deck beneath a grey sky
beats.summary: Hope works his passage across the sea and follows them to Europe.

beats.scene: A map of Europe with pins marking three far-apart cities
beats.summary: He follows them to St Petersburg, Copenhagen and Paris, but he always arrives a day too late.

beats.scene: A pale man in a doctor's office holds his chest and listens
beats.summary: After years of the chase, Hope's health fails, and a doctor tells him he has a serious weakness of the heart.

beats.scene: A thin driver sits on a cab in a foggy London street
beats.summary: In London Hope buys a cab and a horse and becomes a driver, because a cab lets a man follow people without being noticed.

beats.scene: A cab driver watches two men step out of a house in Camberwell
beats.summary: One day Hope spots Drebber and Stangerson and follows them to Madame Charpentier's boarding house.

beats.scene: A cab waits in the dark outside a boarding house on a quiet terrace
beats.summary: For weeks Hope follows them in his cab, but they always go about together, and he can never catch Drebber alone.

beats.scene: A drunk man staggers toward a waiting cab outside a railway station
beats.summary: On the last night Drebber is thrown out of the boarding house, and Hope picks him up, drunk and alone, at Euston station.

beats.scene: A cab stops at a dark, empty house with a for-sale sign
beats.summary: Hope drives to the empty house in Brixton Road, which he knows well, and leads the drunk man inside by the arm.

beats.scene: A man holds up a gold ring in the light of one candle
beats.summary: In the empty room Hope lights a candle, tells Drebber who he is and holds up Lucy's ring in front of his face.

beats.scene: Two small round pills lie in a box on a man's open palm
beats.summary: Hope shows two pills, one harmless and one deadly, and says that Drebber must choose one while he takes the other.

beats.scene: A man lies still on the floor of a bare room beside a candle
beats.summary: Drebber takes a pill, and it is the poison; Hope's nose bleeds from excitement, and he writes the word RACHE.

beats.scene: A cab driver stands at a gate pretending to be drunk before a policeman
beats.summary: Hope realises that he has lost the ring, returns to the house and, when a constable questions him, pretends to be drunk.

beats.scene: A man climbs a ladder at night toward a lit hotel window
beats.summary: Hope finds Stangerson at his hotel, climbs a ladder into his room and stabs him when the man attacks, then writes RACHE.

beats.scene: A pale man speaks calmly to three listeners in a lamplit sitting room
beats.summary: Hope finishes his story, adding that the old woman who came for the ring was a friend of his, and that the ring came back to him.

beats.scene: Two police officers lead a calm man in handcuffs from a house
beats.summary: Hope says he has nothing to be ashamed of, and the police take him away to the station.

beats.scene: A man gives a statement before a row of magistrates in a courtroom
beats.summary: Hope is brought before the magistrates, who are told that he will be tried the next day.

beats.scene: A cell door stands open at dawn, with a still figure on the bed
beats.summary: The morning before the trial, Hope is found dead in his cell, with a peaceful smile on his face.

beats.scene: A doctor leans over a dead man's chest in a plain stone cell
beats.summary: The doctor says the great vessel of his heart burst in the night, as it had long been going to do.

beats.scene: Holmes talks to Watson beside the fire with a pipe in his hand
beats.summary: Holmes explains that most people reason forward, but he reasons backward from the result to the steps that led to it.

beats.scene: A telegram, a pill box and a ring lie on a table
beats.summary: Holmes names the clues that led him to the man: the ring, the cab, the pills and the telegram from Cleveland.

beats.scene: A newspaper on a breakfast table praises two detectives by name
beats.summary: The next day the newspapers say that Gregson and Lestrade solved the case, and they do not mention Holmes.

beats.scene: Watson folds the newspaper and speaks firmly to a smiling Holmes
beats.summary: Holmes laughs at the credit given to others, and Watson says that the public must know the truth, so he will publish it.

beats.scene: A lamp burns at a writing table in a sitting room in Baker Street
beats.summary: Watson writes the story, and Holmes names the case a study in scarlet, a red thread running through the grey of life.

A1A2: John Watson became an army doctor, and a war began in Afghanistan.
At a battle called Maiwand, a bullet hit his shoulder, and Murray saved him.
He nearly died of a fever in a hospital at Peshawar.
A ship brought him home to England, but he was very weak.
He had no family and little money, so he went to London.
In London he lived in a sad hotel, and spent his money.
One day he counted his money and saw that he must move.
In a busy bar, an old friend named Stamford tapped his shoulder.
Stamford saw that Watson was thin and brown, and they had lunch.
Watson needed cheap rooms, and Stamford knew another man who wanted the same.
Stamford said that Sherlock Holmes was a clever man with strange ideas.
Holmes was not a doctor, but he knew a great deal.
Stamford said that Holmes once hit dead bodies with a stick.
He said Holmes might even try a new poison on a friend.
They walked to the hospital, and Stamford looked a little worried.
In a bare room, Holmes bent over a glass tube.
Holmes jumped up with joy and told them he had found something new.
Holmes cut his finger and put a drop of blood in water.
“You have been in Afghanistan, I see,” said Holmes to Watson.
They talked about their bad habits, and then agreed to share rooms.
The next day, they saw the rooms and liked them very much.
Watson moved in that night, and Holmes came the next morning.
Holmes was quiet and left the house early every single day.
Sometimes he lay on the sofa for days and said nothing.
Holmes was very tall and thin, with sharp eyes and a long nose.
Watson wrote a list of what Holmes knew and did not know.
Holmes knew a lot about chemistry, and he was good at boxing.
Holmes also played the violin very well, sometimes slowly and softly.
At breakfast, Holmes told Watson how he knew about Afghanistan.
Many strange people came to see Holmes, and they were all his clients.
Watson found out that Holmes did not know about the sun.
Holmes said that a mind is like a small room.
One dull morning, Watson read a story in a magazine.
The writer said one small thing can show you a big chain.
Watson laughed at it, but Holmes said he wrote it.
Holmes said he was a detective that other detectives ask for help.
He said that all crimes are a little like old ones.
Holmes looked at a man in the street and described him.
The man came in, and Holmes guessed right about his past.
Holmes read his letter quickly, and his eyes became bright.
The letter said a dead man was in an empty house.
Holmes was lazy that morning, but at last he agreed to go.
In the cab, Holmes talked about violins, and Watson felt impatient.
They came to a quiet road and a dirty empty house.
Gregson met them, and Holmes looked at the muddy garden path.
Holmes went down on his hands and knees and looked at the ground.
The front room was empty, dusty, and almost dark.
A well-dressed man lay on the floor, and his face looked very angry.
Gregson showed them the dead man's watch, money, cards, and a book.
Holmes smelled the dead man's lips and found no wound on him.
On the wall, someone had written the word RACHE in blood.
Lestrade said it was the start of a girl's name.
The body moved, and a woman's gold ring rolled on the floor.
Holmes took out a tape and a glass and crawled around.
He found some grey ash on the floor and put it away.
Holmes measured the room, and he knew how tall the killer was.
The killer wore strong boots and he had very long nails.
The killer came in a cab, and his face was red.
The detectives asked how the man died, and Holmes said poison.
At the door, Holmes said that Rache means revenge.
Outside, Watson asked how Holmes knew so many things.
Holmes read the marks on the road, and he knew the cab and horse.
Nothing was taken, so Holmes said the killer wanted revenge.
Holmes sent a message to America to ask about the dead man.
They found the policeman's house in a small, quiet street.
The policeman told them he found the empty house open at night.
After that, he went back to the gate and saw a drunk man.
The drunk man was tall, with a red face and a brown coat.
Holmes paid him some money, but he was very angry with him.
Holmes understood that the killer came back to the house for the ring.
Holmes wrote a notice about a ring, and Watson took it to the papers.
The notice said Watson would give back the ring that evening.
Holmes took Watson to hear a woman play the violin.
That night, Watson waited with the ring, and Holmes sat with a book.
At nine o'clock, a very old woman came up the stairs.
She said the ring was her daughter's, and she was afraid.
Watson gave her the ring, and she went away very quickly.
Holmes put on his coat and ran out after her.
Holmes saw her get into a cab, and he jumped up behind.
The cab was empty, and Holmes said he was beaten.
The next morning, all the newspapers wrote about the dead man.
Holmes laughed at what they said, and he drank his coffee.
Gregson came in, and he said, “I have caught the man.”
He had gone to a house where the dead man lived.
The girl in the house said the dead man was rude to her.
Her brother Arthur had come home late that night with a stick.
Gregson thought that Arthur had followed the man and killed him.
Lestrade ran in with a white face and a bad story.
The second man was missing at night, and a boy saw a ladder.
Stangerson lay dead in his room, and the same word was on the wall.
At the hotel, Holmes saw the same word on the wall.
A small box with two pills was in the room.
Mrs Hudson had an old, sick dog, and Holmes asked for it.
Holmes put the first pill in milk, and the dog drank it.
The dog drank the second one, and it died at once.
Holmes said that one pill was safe and the other was poison.
A message came from America about a man named Jefferson Hope.
Holmes sent some street boys to find a cab.
A driver came to help with a box, and Holmes caught him.
The driver fought hard, and then he became quiet and said he was dying.
There is a great dry desert in the middle of America.
In 1847, a man and a small girl sat by a rock.
The man was John Ferrier, and he had no more water.
The little girl, Lucy, asked where her mother and father were.
John gave her the last drop of water from his flask.
Lucy fell asleep in his arms, and he was afraid.
Far away, he saw a small cloud of dust.
It grew bigger, and he saw a line of wagons.
A rider reached them and gave them cool water to drink.
An old man said that he would take them if they agreed.
John said that he would believe what the old man believed.
A kind woman looked after Lucy, and John became strong again.
The wagons went on for weeks across rivers and mountains.
John was a good hunter, and the people respected him.
At last they came to a green valley by a great lake.
Their leader chose where to build a city in the valley.
John got good land and built a house for Lucy and himself.
John worked hard, and after some years, he was rich.
The Saints told him to take a wife, but he did not.
Lucy grew up happy on the farm, and John loved her.
Thirteen years passed, and Lucy was now a lovely young woman.
One day in May, she rode to town on her horse.
A big herd of cattle ran toward her on the road.
A young hunter on a horse pulled her to safety.
His name was Jefferson Hope, and he had come from Nevada.
Lucy told her father about it, and he thanked Hope.
Hope stayed for some weeks, and he and Lucy fell in love.
He asked her father if he could marry her.
Her father said yes, but he told Hope to come back soon.
Hope rode away, and Lucy waved to him from the gate.
Weeks passed, and Lucy missed Hope very much.
One evening, the Prophet, Brigham Young, rode up to the house.
He said that John had been treated well by the church.
He said that Lucy must marry one of two young men.
John asked for time, and the Prophet gave him thirty days.
The Prophet rode away, and John felt very afraid.
John stayed awake all night and tried to think of a plan.
He told Lucy, and she said that she would never agree.
John sent a secret message to Hope, and it said, “Come quickly.”
The two young men came, and John sent them away.
John counted the days, and he told Lucy to be brave.
One morning, he found a paper with a number on his bed.
The number was twenty-six, and every day it became smaller.
His neighbours would not speak to him, and he felt alone.
John sat up each night with his rifle in his hands.
With three days left, Lucy cried, and there was no news.
Late one night, somebody tapped on the window softly.
It was Jefferson Hope, and he had come in secret.
Hope said they must leave that night, and he told them his plan.
They packed food and water, and left their farm for ever.
At midnight, they left the house and found the horses.
They rode all night without speaking a word.
At the first pass, Hope gave a sign, and the guard let them pass.
At the second place, Hope did the same, and it worked.
When morning came, they left the road and climbed the mountains.
They walked along a narrow path with a deep drop beside it.
Some riders came near, and the three of them hid behind rocks.
They found a hidden place and rested there that night.
Hope said that they needed meat, so he would go hunting.
At dawn, he took his rifle and went up the mountain.
Hope hunted all day, and then he got lost in the hills.
At night, he came back to the hollow and called, but nobody answered.
The camp was empty, and there were many horse tracks all around.
There was a new grave there, with a paper that said, John Ferrier.
Hope sat by the grave and cried, and then he became very angry.
He went back to the valley and met his old friend Cowper.
Cowper told him that Ferrier was dead and Lucy was taken.
Lucy was forced to marry Drebber, who took the farm.
Lucy was so sad that she died within a month.
Hope took the ring from her finger and promised revenge.
Hope ran into the hills and hid there for weeks.
A year later, he came back and found that Drebber was gone.
Hope followed their path across America for years.
He worked in mines and farms, and he never lost hope.
In Cleveland, Hope saw Drebber, but Drebber saw him, too.
Drebber asked the police for help, and Hope went to prison.
When Hope came out, Drebber and Stangerson had left America.
Hope worked on a ship, and sailed to Europe after them.
He followed them to Russia, Denmark and France.
A doctor told him that his heart was very weak.
In London, Hope bought a cab and became a cab driver.
One day, he saw Drebber and followed him to a house.
For weeks, he followed them, but they were never alone.
On the last night, Drebber was alone and drunk at the station.
Hope drove him to an empty house in Brixton Road.
In the dark room, Hope showed him Lucy's ring.
Hope held out two pills and told him to choose one.
Drebber took the bad pill, and he died on the floor.
Hope lost the ring, and he went back and acted drunk.
He found Stangerson, and a fight began that ended in his death.
When Hope finished, he said that his work was done.
He said he felt no shame, and the police took him away.
The next day he spoke to the court, and there was to be a trial.
On the morning before the trial, Hope was found dead in bed.
The doctor said that his heart had broken in the night.
Holmes told Watson that he thinks backward from the end.
He said that the ring, the cab, and the pills showed him the man.
The papers said that Gregson and Lestrade had done everything.
Watson said that he would tell the world the true story.
Watson wrote it all down, and a famous friendship began.
B1B2: John Watson took his degree in medicine in 1878 and then trained to be an army surgeon. Soon afterwards he was sent to India, but a new war had begun in Afghanistan before his ship reached land.
At the battle of Maiwand, a bullet broke the bones of Watson's shoulder. His orderly, a brave man named Murray, threw him across a horse and led him safely back to the British lines.
Watson was taken to the base hospital at Peshawar, where he began to get better. Then he caught a fever that was common among the soldiers, and for months nobody thought he would live.
At last he was strong enough to travel, and a troopship called the Orontes carried him to Portsmouth. His health was ruined, but the government gave him nine months to try to recover.
Watson had no relatives and no friends in England, and his only income was a small army pension. Like many idle people from all over the Empire, he drifted to London.
For a while he lived in a gloomy hotel in the Strand, where he had nothing to do and nobody to talk to. He spent his money far more freely than he should have done.
One morning he looked at his accounts and was alarmed to see how little was left. He knew that he must either leave London altogether or change the way he lived.
He chose to change his way of life, and he decided to look for cheaper rooms the very next day. That same afternoon he was standing in the Criterion Bar when someone touched his shoulder.
It was young Stamford, who had worked under him as a dresser at St Bartholomew's hospital. Stamford was shocked to see him so thin and brown, and he took him to lunch in Holborn.
Over lunch Watson told him about the war, the wound and his search for cheap rooms. Stamford laughed and said it was a strange thing, because Watson was the second man that day to say so.
Stamford said that Sherlock Holmes was a little queer in his ideas, and that he was too keen on some branches of science. As far as he knew, though, Holmes was a decent fellow.
Holmes was not a medical student, and nobody was sure what he meant to do in life. But he knew a great deal about anatomy and chemistry, and his odd knowledge would have surprised his teachers.
Stamford added that Holmes wanted exact knowledge about everything, and sometimes he went too far. He had once seen him beating bodies in the dissecting room, to learn how bruises form after death.

He could be cold-blooded too, said Stamford, and he could imagine Holmes giving a friend a little of some new poison. It would not be from malice, but only to learn what it did, and he would take it himself as readily.
Stamford took Watson to the hospital, but he would not promise anything. “If you quarrel,” he said, “you must take your own risks, because I will not be blamed.”
They found Holmes alone in a long laboratory, bent over a test tube. Hearing them come in, he sprang up with a shout of joy and cried that he had found it.
He explained that he had found a chemical that was affected by blood and by nothing else. It would show an old stain on a coat as surely as a fresh one, and it would help many cases in court.
To prove it, Holmes pricked his finger and let a drop of blood fall into a large jar of clear water. In a moment the water turned a dull brown colour, and a little brown dust settled at the bottom.
Stamford introduced them, and Holmes shook Watson's hand warmly. Then, looking at him closely, he said, “You have been in Afghanistan, I perceive,” and Watson stared at him in astonishment.
Holmes would not say how he knew, but he spoke at once about the rooms he had found. Each man told the other his faults, and they agreed to meet at Baker Street next day.
The next day the two men met and looked at the rooms in Baker Street. There were two bedrooms and a large, bright sitting room, and the price was so low when shared that they took it at once.

That evening Watson moved in his bags from the hotel, and Holmes followed the next morning with several boxes and cases. For a day or two they were busy unpacking, while their landlady, Mrs Hudson, brought them tea and watched them with a kind smile.

Holmes was not hard to live with, because his habits were regular and he made little noise. He was usually out before Watson woke, working at the laboratory, in the dissecting rooms or on long walks through the poorest streets.

When he was not working, Holmes sometimes lay on the sofa for days without speaking or moving. Watson saw the dreamy, empty look in his eyes, but his clean, careful way of life made the idea of drugs impossible.

Anybody would have noticed Holmes's appearance, because he was over six feet tall and so lean that he looked taller. He had bright eyes and a thin, hawk-like nose, and his stained fingers were surprisingly delicate.

One evening Watson, curious, wrote a list of what his friend knew and did not know. Under literature, philosophy and astronomy he wrote the word nothing, and under politics he wrote that Holmes was weak.

On the other side of the list, he wrote that Holmes was deep in chemistry, and that he knew British law well. He also knew every detail of every famous crime of the century, and he was a fine boxer and swordsman and a skilful violin player.

Holmes's violin playing puzzled Watson, because it was sometimes sweet and sometimes strange. In the evenings he would lean back with closed eyes and play soft music, then suddenly stop and begin something wild and cheerful.

Over breakfast Watson at last asked how Holmes had known about Afghanistan, and Holmes explained that he had read the signs quickly. Watson said he sounded like Dupin, but Holmes replied that Dupin was a poor fellow, and Lecoq a bungler.

Visitors began to come to the rooms: a rat-faced little man called Lestrade, a smart girl, an old pedlar and a railway porter. Each time Holmes asked Watson to give up the sitting room, saying that these people were his clients.

Watson was shocked to find that Holmes did not know that the earth goes round the sun. Holmes said that a man's brain is like a small empty attic, and that a wise man chooses carefully what to put in it.
A fool, said Holmes, fills his attic with every kind of rubbish, until the useful things are lost. If we went round the moon instead, he said, it would make no difference to him or to his work.
One dull morning, while Holmes was still in bed, Watson sat reading a magazine by the window. He found an article called The Book of Life, and read it twice with growing annoyance.
The writer said that a clever thinker could tell the whole story of a river from one drop of water. In the same way, he said, all of life is a long chain, and one link can show you the rest.

He said that a man's trade could be read from his fingernails, his coat sleeve, his boots and his hands. Watson threw down the magazine and called it ineffable twaddle, until Holmes said quietly from the door that he had written it.
Holmes explained that he was the only consulting detective in the world. When the police detectives or private ones were at a loss, they brought him their facts, and he put them on the right track.

He said that crimes had a family likeness, so that a man who knew a thousand of them could often solve the thousand and first. Lestrade was a well-known detective who had come to him over a forgery, and private agencies sent him most of his clients.
Watson said he found it hard to believe a man could solve a mystery from his chair. Holmes smiled and pointed at a broad man in the street, and said he was a retired sergeant of Marines.
Watson laughed, but a moment later the man knocked at the door and handed Holmes a letter. When Holmes asked if he was a sergeant of Marines, the man was amazed, for he was exactly that.

Holmes explained that the man had a blue anchor tattooed on his hand, a soldier's side-whiskers and a commanding air. Then he tore open the letter and read it with the eager look of a man who sees a puzzle.

Gregson's letter said that Enoch Drebber, from Cleveland in America, had been found dead in an empty house, with no wound and nothing stolen. Holmes said that Gregson and Lestrade were the best of a bad lot, and as jealous of each other as two beautiful women.
Holmes at first said he was far too lazy to go, because the police would take the credit anyway. Then he put on his coat, saying he might have a laugh at them if he had nothing else.

In the cab Holmes talked cheerfully about violins, the old town of Cremona and the great Stradivarius. When Watson asked why he gave the case so little thought, he replied that it was a mistake to guess before one had facts.
They came to Brixton Road, where a dull house stood back from the street, with an empty garden in front. Some idlers stood at the gate, hoping to see something, though a policeman kept them back.

In the middle of North America there lies a great dry desert, which was once an enemy to every traveller. Nothing grows there but a few bitter bushes, and for hundreds of miles there is neither water nor shade.
On the fourth of May 1847, a worn and hungry man sat down beside a rock in this desert. He was John Ferrier, and in his arms lay a little girl of about five, with a face as white as paper.
Ferrier's mules had died, his water was gone, and the others in his party had fallen one by one on the long road. He and the child were the only ones left, and he had no idea where to find help.
The little girl looked up and asked where her mother and father were, and when they would come. Ferrier told her sadly that they had gone away, and that he would look after her now.
He had one mouthful of water left in his flask, and he held it to the child's lips. She drank it all, and he did not take a drop himself.
Soon Lucy fell asleep with her head on his shoulder, and the sun began to go down. Ferrier thought quietly that neither of them would see the morning.
As he stared out across the plain, he saw a faint cloud of white dust, far away to the east. He could not tell what it was, and he was too weak to stand up.

The cloud grew bigger, and at last Ferrier could see that it was made by a very long line of wagons with white covers. Hundreds of men and animals were moving slowly across the desert toward the west.
A horseman rode ahead of the train and found them lying by the rock. He gave them water from his flask, a little at a time, and then lifted them up and carried them to the wagons.

The leader of the wagons was an elder with a stern face and a plain coat, and he asked who they were. He said that his people were Saints, followers of a prophet, and he would take them with him only if they accepted his faith.

Ferrier was too tired to argue, and he said that he would follow any faith that saved the child. The elder nodded coldly and told him that he and Lucy might ride in the wagons, but that he would be watched.
A kind woman took Lucy into her wagon and wrapped her in warm blankets. Day by day Ferrier grew stronger, and the child began to smile again.
The wagon train crawled on for weeks, across wide rivers and over steep mountains. The Saints were people of great courage, and they worked together without complaint.
Ferrier found that he was a better hunter than most of them, and he often rode ahead of the train to find game. The Saints began to respect him, even though he was a stranger.
At last the train came to a broad green valley, with a great salt lake shining in the distance. Their Prophet, Brigham Young, said that this was the place that had been promised to them.
The Prophet planned a city, marked out in squares with sticks driven into the ground. Each family was given land according to its place in the church, so that the chief men received the best.
Ferrier was given a good piece of land, because he had proved himself on the road. He built a log house with his own hands, and it was snug enough for himself and Lucy.
Ferrier was clever with soil and tireless in his work, and his fields grew rich and green. Within a few years he was one of the richest farmers in the whole valley.
The Saints expected every man to take several wives, and they often urged Ferrier to do the same. He refused, and though he never said why, his neighbours began to whisper about it.
Lucy grew up happy and healthy on the farm, with the sun and the open air as her friends. Ferrier loved her as dearly as if she had been his own daughter, and she loved him in return.
Thirteen years went by, and Lucy grew into a tall, beautiful young woman, with a brown face and bright eyes. Everyone in the valley knew her as the Flower of Utah.
One morning in May 1860, she rode into town on her best horse to buy some things for the farm. At the same moment a huge herd of cattle came pouring down the road from the plains.
The herd was wild and noisy, and the cattle ran in every direction. Lucy's horse was caught in the middle, and she could not turn it round, so she was in great danger of being trampled.
A young hunter on a strong horse rode in through the dust and caught Lucy's bridle. He pulled her through the crowd of horns, and a moment later they were safe at the side of the road.
The stranger took off his hat, and Lucy saw that he was tall and brown, with a cheerful face. He told her that his name was Jefferson Hope, and that he had come from the silver mines of Nevada.
When Lucy told her father the story, Ferrier shook Hope's hand warmly and thanked him with tears in his eyes. He asked him to come and stay at the farm for as long as he liked.
Hope stayed for weeks, and he and Lucy walked together under the stars on warm evenings. Before long they both knew that they were deeply in love.
One night Hope spoke to Ferrier by the fire and asked if he might marry Lucy. Ferrier was glad, but he was also afraid, because he knew that the elders would never approve of an outsider.
At last Ferrier said that he would agree, if Hope would go back to Nevada and earn some money first. If he came back in two months, he could take Lucy away from the valley.
Hope promised, and he swore to come back as fast as his horse could carry him. Lucy stood at the gate, waving, until he was a speck on the road, and then she turned back to the house in tears.

The Prophet sat down at the table, and for a long moment he said nothing. Then he told Ferrier coldly that he had been treated well by the church, though he had never truly joined it.

He said that Lucy was now of an age to marry, and that he had chosen two husbands for her. She might pick either the son of Elder Stangerson or the son of Elder Drebber, but she must marry one of them.

Ferrier begged for a little time, saying that Lucy was young and had not been brought up in that way. The Prophet gave him thirty days to decide, and warned him that the church punishes those who disobey.

In the morning he told Lucy everything the Prophet had said. She turned white, but she took his hand and said bravely that she would die before she married either of the two young men.

Ferrier marked the days one by one on a calendar, and every night he told Lucy to keep her courage. He tried to smile, but he knew that the time was running out.

The neighbours who had once been friendly now turned their backs when he came near. Nobody in the valley would speak to him, and Ferrier felt that hidden eyes were watching every step he took.
He began to sit up at night by the window with his rifle across his knees. Nothing ever came, but the numbers on the wall grew smaller each morning.

He told Watson that the ring had shown him a woman and a motive, and the cab and the marks had told him the man. The pills and the telegram from Cleveland had given him the rest.
