He told Watson that he would wash his hands of the whole affair if the two of them fell out, and that Watson must take his own risks. Then, with a rueful smile and a shake of his head, he led the way along a gloomy corridor that smelled of chemicals.

In a long, bare laboratory, strewn with bottles and test tubes, a tall figure was bending eagerly over a table at the far end. Hearing their footsteps, he sprang up with a cry of pleasure and shouted that he had found it, that he had found it at last. He came towards them holding a test tube, and his eyes shone like those of a hunter who has seen the track.

He had discovered, he told them, a reagent that was affected by haemoglobin and by nothing else, which was a discovery of great practical value. Surely, he said, a man might now tell a stain of blood from rust or fruit juice, even after months, and many a criminal had escaped for want of such a test. He spoke so earnestly that he seemed to be addressing a court of law.

To prove it, Holmes took a long needle, pricked his finger and drew a drop of blood into a chemical pipette. He then dropped it into a jar holding a litre of water, which at first looked as pure as it had been before. In a few moments, however, the water turned the colour of dull mahogany, and a brownish dust began to settle at the bottom.

Stamford presented Watson with a friendly word, and Holmes seized his hand with surprising warmth, his grip as strong as his body was thin. Then, looking him over from head to foot, he said calmly, “You have been in Afghanistan, I perceive.” Watson was so astonished that for a moment he could say nothing at all.

Holmes only smiled when Watson demanded how he had known it, and turned to the matter of the rooms that he had found in Baker Street. Each man frankly confessed his faults, Holmes owning that he played the violin, smoked strong tobacco and sometimes sat sunk in silence for days, while Watson spoke of his lazy ways and his poor nerves. They found that they suited each other well, and they agreed to meet at noon next day, to see the place.

Next day the two men met as they had agreed, and walked round the rooms at 221B Baker Street, which Holmes had mentioned at the laboratory. There were two comfortable bedrooms and a single large, airy sitting room, cheerfully furnished and lit by two broad windows. So desirable were the rooms, and so moderate the rent when it was divided between them, that the bargain was settled on the spot.

That very evening Watson moved his few possessions from the hotel, and on the following morning Holmes arrived with several boxes and portmanteaus. For a day or two they were busy unpacking and laying out their belongings to the best advantage, while the landlady, Mrs Hudson, bustled up and down the stairs with trays of tea. By degrees they settled down and learned to accommodate themselves to their new surroundings.

Holmes proved to be no difficult man to live with, for he was quiet in his ways and regular in his habits. It was rare for him to be up after ten at night, and he had invariably breakfasted and gone out before Watson rose in the morning. Some days he spent at the chemical laboratory, some in the dissecting rooms, and others in long walks that seemed to lead him into the lowest quarters of the city.

Nothing could exceed his energy when the working fit was upon him, but now and again a reaction seized him, and he would lie upon the sofa for days, hardly uttering a word or moving a muscle. On such occasions Watson saw such a dreamy, vacant expression in his eyes that he might have suspected him of some narcotic habit. But the temperance and cleanliness of his whole life, which Watson saw day after day, forbade the notion.

The man's very person was enough to strike the attention of the most casual observer, for he stood rather over six feet and was so excessively lean that he seemed taller still. His eyes were sharp and piercing, save during those intervals of torpor, and his thin, hawk-like nose gave his whole face an air of alertness and decision. His hands were always blotted with ink and stained with chemicals, yet he had an extraordinary delicacy of touch.

As his curiosity grew, Watson drew up a list of his friend's accomplishments, headed with the title of Sherlock Holmes, his limits. Literature, philosophy and astronomy he marked as nil, politics as feeble, and botany as variable, since Holmes knew poisons well but nothing of gardens. It struck him that never had a man gathered so strange a collection of knowledge, or so carefully left out everything else.

The list went on to note that his geology was practical, for he could tell one soil from another at a glance, and that his chemistry was profound. His anatomy was accurate but unsystematic, and his reading in sensational literature was immense, so that he seemed to know every horror perpetrated in the century. Finally he was an expert at singlestick, boxing and swordsmanship, and had a good practical knowledge of British law.

There was the matter of the violin, which Holmes played with remarkable skill but in a very curious way. At times he would draw from it soft, sweet melodies that must have been in his mind for hours, and at others he would scrape out wild and cheerful fragments that had no tune at all. Leaning back in his armchair with closed eyes, he seemed to Watson more of a riddle than ever.

Holmes explained at last, over a cup of coffee, that the chain of thoughts had run so swiftly through his mind that he had reached his conclusion without being aware of the steps. He had seen a man of medical type with the air of a soldier, tanned in the face but fair at the wrists, thin from sickness and holding his left arm stiffly. When Watson compared him to Poe's Dupin, Holmes answered coolly that Dupin was a very inferior fellow, and that Lecoq was a miserable bungler.

As the weeks passed, Watson noticed an odd stream of visitors, among them a sallow, rat-faced little man whom Holmes introduced as Mr Lestrade, a fashionable young girl and a seedy old pedlar. Each time Holmes begged the use of the sitting room, and Watson went off to his bedroom, while his friend apologised politely for the trouble. Holmes at last explained that he used the room as a place of business, and that these odd people were his clients.

Watson was amazed one evening to discover that Holmes did not know that the earth travels round the sun, a fact that every schoolboy knows. When he mentioned it, Holmes replied with a shrug that a man's brain was originally like a little empty attic, which he must stock with such furniture as he chooses. A fool, he said, takes in all the lumber he comes across, until the useful knowledge is crowded out.

The skilful workman, Holmes went on, is very careful about what he takes into his brain-attic, and he will have nothing but the tools that may help him in his work. He insisted that every addition crowds out something that he knew before, and that it is of the highest importance not to have useless facts elbowing out the useful ones. As for the solar system, he said, if we went round the moon, it would not make a pennyworth of difference to him or to his work.

Some days later, on a dull and dreary morning, Watson picked up a magazine from the table while Holmes lingered in bed. He found an article in it with the title of The Book of Life, and he read it through twice, becoming more irritated at every paragraph. It seemed to him a strange mixture of clever remarks and plain absurdity, and he threw it down at last with impatience.

The writer argued that a logician, given a single drop of water, might infer the possibility of an Atlantic or a Niagara without having seen or heard of either. All life, he claimed, is a great chain, the nature of which is known whenever we are shown a single link of it. Like every other art, the science of deduction and analysis could be acquired only by long and patient study, and no mortal was likely to master it entirely.

The article went on to say that by a man's finger nails, his coat sleeve, his boots, his trouser knees and the calluses on his forefinger and thumb, his calling is plainly revealed. Watson cried out that it was the most ineffable twaddle he had ever read, and that the writer was a mere armchair theorist who had never tested his ideas. At this Holmes, who had entered the room unseen, remarked mildly that he had written it himself.

Holmes told him calmly that he had a trade of his own, and that he supposed he was the only man in the world who followed it. He called himself a consulting detective, and explained that London had plenty of government detectives and plenty of private ones, and that when these fellows were at fault, they came to him. They laid all the evidence before him, and he generally set them on the right track by the help of his knowledge of the history of crime.

There is a strong family resemblance about misdeeds, he said, and if you have the details of a thousand at your fingertips, it is odd if you cannot unravel the thousand and first. Lestrade, he explained, was a well-known detective who had lately got himself into a fog over a forgery case, and that was what had brought him to the rooms. As for the rest of the visitors, they were mostly sent by private inquiry agencies, and Holmes listened to their stories, offered his comments and then pocketed his fee.

Watson, unconvinced, said that he could not believe that a man could unravel a knot without leaving his room, though others had seen every detail for themselves. Holmes, with a trace of annoyance, led him to the window and pointed out a stout man in the street below, who was looking carefully at the numbers on the houses and carrying a large blue envelope. Without any hesitation, he said that the man was a retired sergeant of Marines.

Watson thought that his friend was merely boasting, since he knew that Holmes could never be asked to prove such a guess. But hardly had the thought crossed his mind when the man in the street ran up the steps, and a loud knock echoed through the house. A moment later the stranger entered with a letter in his hand, and when Holmes asked whether he had been a sergeant of Marines, he said, much astonished, that he had.

When the man had left the room, Holmes explained that a blue anchor was tattooed on the back of his hand, which suggested the sea, and that he had a military carriage and regulation side-whiskers. He also held his head with an air of command and carried himself with a steady, respectable swagger, so that Holmes had concluded he was no ordinary soldier. Watson could only exclaim that it was wonderful, and then he saw his friend tear open the envelope with a very eager look.

The note, which Holmes read aloud, was brief and polite, and it told how a constable had found a well-dressed gentleman dead in an empty house in Brixton Road, with the name of Enoch Drebber of Cleveland on his cards. There was no wound upon him and nothing had been stolen, though there were marks of blood in the room. Gregson, said Holmes, was the smartest of the Scotland Yarders, and he and Lestrade were the pick of a bad lot, quick and energetic but conventional, and as jealous of each other as a pair of professional beauties.

Holmes did not stir from his chair, and he declared that he was the most incurably lazy devil that ever stood in shoe leather, at least when the fit was on him. Supposing he unravelled the whole matter, he said, Gregson and Lestrade would pocket all the credit, which was the penalty of being an unofficial person. Yet after a moment he rose, saying that he might have a laugh at them, if he had nothing else, and they set off together.

The four-wheeled cab rattled across London, and Holmes, to Watson's irritation, talked cheerfully about Cremona fiddles and the difference between a Stradivarius and an Amati. Watson at last remarked that he seemed to give very little thought to the matter in hand. Holmes answered that it was a capital mistake to theorise before one had data, since it biased the judgment and led one to twist facts to suit theories.

Their cab turned into Brixton Road, a dreary street of dull houses, and stopped at number three, which stood a little back from the pavement. It was a tenantless place with a dirty garden in front and yellow bills in the windows, and a small crowd had gathered at the gate, craning their necks. A constable in uniform stood on the steps, keeping them back with a stolid, official look.

Gregson met them with a self-satisfied air, rubbing his hands, and said that he had left everything untouched until Holmes should arrive. Holmes pointed to the garden path, which was a mass of trampled mud, and observed that if a herd of buffaloes had passed along it, there could not be a greater mess. Gregson replied evasively that he had been busy inside, and that he had relied upon his colleague, Mr Lestrade, to look after the path.

Holmes glanced at Watson and raised his eyebrows, then asked whether either of the officers had come to the house by cab, and both said that they had not. He knelt at the gate and then bent over the garden path, murmuring to himself, with his lens in his hand and his nose almost on the ground. Watson, who watched him, thought that he had never seen such patient and eager attention given to a patch of mud.

The front room was large and square, and it looked larger still because there was not a stick of furniture in it. A vulgar paper adorned the walls, but it was blotched with mildew, and strips had come loose and hung down, showing the yellow plaster beneath. On the mantelpiece stood the stump of a red wax candle, and the one dirty window let in a dull grey light.

On the floor lay a man about forty-three or forty-four years of age, middle-sized and broad shouldered, with crisp black hair and a short stubbly beard. He was dressed in a heavy frock coat and light trousers, with immaculate collar and cuffs, and a well-brushed top hat lay on the floor beside him. His hands were clenched, and on his rigid face there was an expression of horror and, as it seemed to Watson, of hatred, such as he had never seen on a human face.

Gregson read out what had been found in the dead man's pockets: a gold watch and chain, a card case with the name of Enoch Drebber, and a few pounds in loose money. There was also a small pocket edition of Boccaccio, which bore the name of Joseph Stangerson on the flyleaf, and there were two letters, one addressed to each man. It was clear, said Gregson, that the man had not been robbed, whatever else might have been done to him.

Holmes knelt beside the body, ran his nimble fingers over it and bent close to sniff the dead man's lips. There was no wound on him anywhere, though the floor around him was splashed with blood. That blood, Holmes said quietly, must therefore belong to a second person, very probably the murderer.

On the wall, in a corner where the paper had peeled away, someone had scrawled a single word in dark red letters. It was RACHE, and the letters were smeared and uneven, as if they had been written in a hurry with a finger dipped in blood. Gregson pointed at it with a flourish, like a showman who had arranged a surprise for his visitor.

Lestrade, who had joined them, announced with great confidence that the word was clearly the beginning of the female name Rachel. The writer, he explained, had been disturbed before he had time to finish, and so the police ought to look for a woman of that name. Both detectives seemed delighted with this theory, and they glanced at Holmes to see how it was received.

When the body was lifted for examination, something fell from beneath it, and a woman's plain gold wedding ring rolled across the bare floor with a tinkle. Gregson picked it up and declared with excitement that this changed the whole case, since it must belong to a woman. Holmes made no reply, though he looked at the little circle of gold for a long time.

Holmes now drew a long tape measure and a large round magnifying glass from his pocket, and with these he trotted noiselessly about the room. Sometimes he stopped, sometimes he knelt, and once he lay flat upon his face, chattering under his breath in a stream of little exclamations, groans and whistles. He was so engrossed that he seemed to have forgotten that anybody else was present.

From the floor he gathered a little pile of grey dust and shut it carefully in an envelope, which he slipped into his pocket. He studied the footprints in the dust, and it seemed to Watson that he read them as a scholar reads a manuscript. Then he went to the wall, and measured the letters from top to bottom, and walked round the room once more.

The man who wrote the word, he said, must have stood more than six feet high, and a man of such a height takes a stride of a certain length. He had calculated it from the footsteps, and the writing agreed with it, for a man will generally write on a wall at about the height of his own eyes. It was a simple piece of reasoning, and he gave it as though it were obvious.

The murderer wore coarse, square-toed boots, he said, and his feet were small for his height, as the prints showed plainly. Some scratches in the plaster beneath the word showed that the fingernail of his right hand was remarkably long. The rest of the clues were of the same kind, small in themselves, but when joined together, they made a chain that led straight to the man.

He said the man had come to the house with his victim in a four-wheeled cab, drawn by a horse with three old shoes and one new shoe on its off fore-leg. In all probability the murderer had a florid face, since the blood on the floor had come from his nose. These were only a few indications, Holmes said, but they might help the police.

Lestrade and Gregson exchanged incredulous smiles, as if a child had been telling them a fairy tale. At last Lestrade asked, with a touch of mockery, how the man had been killed, if he had been murdered at all. “Poison,” said Holmes curtly, and he strode towards the door without another word of explanation.

On the threshold, however, he turned round and held up one finger, with a look of lazy amusement that annoyed both detectives. He said that there was one other thing, and that it might save them a good deal of trouble if they listened. Rache, he told them, was the German word for revenge, and so they should not lose their time looking for Miss Rachel.

Out in the road, Watson confessed that he had never seen anything like the display he had just witnessed, and he asked how Holmes had come by it all. Holmes replied that the splashes of blood on the floor had been far too much to come from the dead man, who had no wound. They must have come from the murderer's nose, he said, which suggested a man of strong and florid colour, for such a man bleeds easily.

The road itself, he explained, was a better page of print than the house, for in the soft mud before the gate there were two parallel ruts, deep and clear. They belonged to a cab, since no private carriage would have stopped at such a house at such an hour. The prints of the horse's hoofs showed that three of the shoes were worn, while one was almost new, and a man who has trained his eye will find that the commonest street is full of information.

Nothing had been taken from the dead man, Holmes continued, neither his gold watch nor his money, so there could be no question of robbery as a motive. A crime without gain suggests a crime of passion, and the writing on the wall, he said, had probably been put there to throw the police off the scent. He doubted that any German was concerned in the matter, though he allowed that the word might yet prove useful.

On the way home Holmes stopped at a post office, where he wrote out and sent a long telegram to the police authorities of the American city of Cleveland. He asked whether Enoch Drebber had ever been married, and whether any person had threatened or pursued him in that place. It was a small step, as he remarked to Watson, but it was the sort of step that on occasion decided a whole case.

Later in the day, having found the address from a constable at the station, they made their way to Audley Court, off Kennington Lane. It was a narrow and dismal little place with a row of small houses, and in one of them they found John Rance, the constable who had first discovered the body. He was sitting in his shirt sleeves at his kitchen table, and he welcomed them gruffly, evidently thinking that they were from the newspapers.

He had been on his beat in Brixton Road, Rance told them, and everything had been quiet until one in the morning, when he noticed a light in the window of the empty house. He knew that the house was empty, and so he tried the door and found it open, and he stepped inside with his lantern in his hand. In the front room he saw the dead man lying on the floor, and he went out again at once to blow his whistle.

When he came back to the gate, he said, he found that a drunken man was leaning against the railings, singing at the top of his voice a song called Columbine's New-fangled Banner. The fellow could hardly stand, much less help, and Rance and Murcher had to prop him up between them. They had so much to do that they gave him no more attention than they could help.

Holmes questioned him closely about the man, and Rance replied that he had been a long fellow with a red face, with the lower part of it muffled up in a brown overcoat. He had carried no whip, Rance added, and he had not noticed any cab, either at that moment or afterwards. The constable thought that the drunkard had found his way home safely, as such men generally do.

Holmes stood up and laid half a sovereign on the table, then took his hat and shook his head sadly at the constable. He said that he was afraid Rance would never rise in the force, since his head should be used as well as worn for ornament. He might have gained his sergeant's stripes that night, for the man he had held in his hands was the very man who held the clue to this mystery.

As the door closed behind them, Holmes muttered that he had been a fool not to see it sooner, and Watson asked what he meant. The murderer, he explained, must have discovered that he had left the wedding ring behind him, and had gone back to the house to look for it. It seemed to him that a ring so carelessly dropped might be the very thing that would draw the man out of hiding.

Holmes wrote out a short advertisement in a firm, neat hand and handed it to Watson, with a request that he should take it to every newspaper in London. It stated that a plain gold wedding ring had been found in the roadway of Brixton Road, between a tavern and Holland Grove, and that the owner might claim it. Watson took it round to the offices of the Daily News and the Standard that same afternoon.

Holmes had very carefully left his own name out of the advertisement, for he thought that the murderer might know it, and had put Watson's name there instead. The owner of the ring was asked to call at Baker Street between eight and nine that evening, and to bring proof of the claim. It was a plain invitation, as Holmes remarked, and it was nobody's business but the owner's to answer it.

With several hours to spare before the visitor was due, Holmes proposed to Watson that they should go to a concert at Hallé's, where a famous lady was to play the violin. Watson was astonished to see him a changed man, for the cold and clever detective became gentle, absorbed and dreamy, beating time with his long fingers while a smile of pure pleasure lit his face. It was an unexpected and rather touching glimpse of the other side of his friend.

They came home for an early supper, and Watson, as agreed, sat by the lamp with the ring on the table before him, while Holmes took a book into a shadowy corner of the room. Neither of them said much, and every footstep in the street made Watson look up with a start. Holmes seemed calm, but he turned the same page of his book several times without reading it.

A little before nine, there was a gentle knock at the door of the sitting room, and Mrs Hudson showed in an old woman, bent almost double. She had a face like a withered apple, a shawl drawn over her head and a stick that rattled on the boards as she came. She peered about the room with sharp little eyes, curtseyed to Watson and said that she had come about the ring that had been found.

In a thin, shaking voice she began a long story, and she explained that the ring belonged to her daughter Sally, who was married to a steward on one of the Union boats. If her son-in-law should learn that the ring had been lost, she said, he would be in such a rage that she dared not think of it. She had been at a dance, she thought, or perhaps at the theatre, and had lost it on the way home.

Watson, finding the account perfectly natural, handed her the ring, and she gave him the address where her daughter lived, a house in Duncan Street, Houndsditch. She seemed to pour out her thanks with half a dozen blessings, bobbing and curtseying in the doorway, and then she turned and went hurrying down the stairs. He could not help observing that for so old a woman she moved with remarkable speed.

The front door had scarcely closed before Holmes was on his feet, throwing on his ulster and winding a scarf about his neck. He told Watson in a few words that the old woman was almost certainly an accomplice, and that he must not let her get away. Then he plunged down the stairs, and Watson, left alone beside the lamp, could only wonder what sort of chase would follow.

It was an hour or more before Holmes returned, and he described how he had kept at a careful distance until the woman reached the end of the road and called a passing cab. As it rattled away he had sprung up lightly behind, and clung there through street after street, expecting every moment that the cab would draw up at the address she had given. It had been, he said wryly, the most uncomfortable and the most foolish ride of his whole life.

When the cab drew up at last at the house in Duncan Street, Holmes dropped down from behind and opened the door, ready to seize his prey. The inside was empty, and the driver, who had been told to drive to that very street, swore that he had never seen his passenger get out. No one at the address had heard of any such person as the old woman, and Holmes had to confess that he had been beaten.

The next morning every newspaper in London was full of the Brixton mystery, and Watson read them aloud over his breakfast. The Standard declared that nothing like it had ever been known, and that the dead man's German name and the writing on the wall pointed to political refugees and secret societies. The Daily News, for its part, blamed the police for letting such a crime happen at all.

Holmes laughed heartily over these theories, saying that the whole business was a joke and that the writers were all wrong. Whatever happened, he told Watson, the credit would go to Gregson and Lestrade, and he would have nothing to show for the trouble but a good laugh. He seemed completely content with this arrangement, and he lit his pipe with perfect calm.

Gregson arrived a little later, in the highest spirits, rubbing his hands and beaming at them as if he had come into a fortune. “I wish you would congratulate me, Mr Holmes,” he said, “for I have made the whole thing as clear as day.” Holmes, with a slight raising of his eyebrows, asked who he supposed the murderer to be.

He had made his way, Gregson told them, to Madame Charpentier's boarding house in Torquay Terrace, Camberwell, where Drebber and Stangerson had lodged for three weeks. The lady was a respectable widow with two children, a daughter named Alice, a pretty girl of nineteen, and a son named Arthur, who was a sub-lieutenant in the navy. Both of them, as he found, had good reason to be uneasy about their late lodger.

Alice told him, with tears in her eyes, that Drebber was a coarse and violent man who often came home drunk, and that on one occasion he had caught her roughly by the arm. Her brother Arthur came in at that very moment, and in a fury he had beaten the American with a heavy stick and thrown him out into the street. Drebber had gone away muttering threats, though none of them had taken them seriously.

On the evening of the murder, Gregson went on, the two Americans had left the house in a hurry to catch the Liverpool train from Euston station. Arthur had gone out later and was not seen again until after midnight, when he came home looking wild and carrying his heavy stick. He could give no account of where he had been, and that, said Gregson, was enough to hang a dozen men.

Gregson concluded that the young man had followed Drebber and quarrelled with him, and had killed him in the empty house in a sudden rage. He leaned back in his chair with the air of a man who has solved the greatest puzzle of his age. Holmes listened with a curious smile, and then said politely that he had a great deal to learn, and would certainly go far.

At that moment the door burst open, and Lestrade, usually so cool and neat, rushed in with his hat awry and his face as white as paper. He gasped that something terrible had happened, and that Mr Joseph Stangerson, the dead man's secretary, had been found murdered at Halliday's Private Hotel. Gregson sprang up in horror, and his fine theory seemed to crumble in the air before their eyes.

Lestrade gave them the facts in a rush: Stangerson had gone out in the evening to look for his friend, and he had come back late to the hotel. Early in the morning, a milk-boy had noticed a ladder, which usually lay in the yard, raised against an open window on the second floor. Looking back, he had seen a man come quietly down it, so openly that the boy had taken him for some workman and thought nothing more about it.

The porter, uneasy, had gone up to the room, and there on the floor lay Stangerson, who had been dead for some hours. He had been stabbed with a knife, and there was no sign of any struggle in the room that could not be explained by the stabbing itself. On the wall above the body, in letters of blood, was written the word RACHE, exactly as in the house in Brixton Road.

At Halliday's Private Hotel, Holmes went straight to the room where Stangerson lay and spent a long time before the writing on the wall. It was the very same word, in the very same letters, and he declared that it was beyond any doubt the work of the same hand. He turned to Lestrade and said gravely that the man who killed Drebber had also killed Stangerson.

Lestrade had also found something in the room, and he showed it to Holmes with a puzzled air. It was a small round box, the kind in which a chemist keeps pills, and inside it lay two little pills of a dull grey colour. Holmes took it carefully in his fingers and said that it was the most important clue they had yet seen.

Back at Baker Street, Holmes asked Mrs Hudson for the loan of her old terrier, which had been sick for a long time and which she had begged Watson to put out of its pain the day before. The poor little creature lay wheezing in its basket, with a muzzle as grey as a miser's beard, and it seemed that it had not long to live. Holmes took it up gently and carried it to the hearthrug, where he set it down with great care.

He cut one of the pills neatly in two and dissolved a half in a saucer of milk, which he then set down before the dog. The terrier lapped it eagerly, licked the saucer clean and lay back on the rug with no more than a contented sigh. Watson waited for some effect, but there was none, and the animal went on breathing as before.

Holmes frowned at this and did not speak, but he took the second pill and treated it in exactly the same way. Hardly had the milk touched the dog's tongue when it gave a convulsive jerk in every limb and fell over, as rigid and lifeless as if it had been struck by lightning. Holmes drew a long breath and wiped his forehead, for he had been quite certain how it would end.

One pill was harmless and the other was poison, he explained, and nobody could have told them apart by looking at them. That, he said, was the horrible cleverness of it, for the murderer had offered each of his victims a choice, and chance alone had to decide who should live. It was a stage in the murderer's revenge, and the man who drew the deadly pill had been made to understand at last why he was punished.

A telegram arrived from the police of Cleveland, and Holmes read it with the greatest satisfaction before he passed it to Watson. It stated that Enoch Drebber had once appealed to the law for protection against a rival in love, one Jefferson Hope, who was at that moment in Europe. The name was the missing piece in the puzzle, and Holmes tapped the paper with his finger, saying that now they had only to find the man.

Holmes now called in Wiggins, the leader of a gang of dirty street boys known as the Baker Street Irregulars, and sent them out across London to find a cab. He described the horse and the sort of driver who might be wanted, and gave them a shilling each, with a guinea to the boy who found him. By evening Wiggins had returned in triumph, saying that the cab had been found, and that the driver was ready to come.

The cabman, it was arranged, should be told that a gentleman wanted a trunk carried downstairs, and he came up the stairs with a stolid, dull face. Gregson and Lestrade stood quietly behind the door, and Watson waited by the fire, hardly daring to breathe. As the man stooped over the trunk, the handcuffs clicked cleanly upon his wrists, and the whole thing was done in an instant.

“Gentlemen,” said Holmes with a smile, “allow me to introduce you to Mr Jefferson Hope, the murderer of Enoch Drebber and of Joseph Stangerson.” The man, a powerful fellow, struggled so desperately that he smashed a pane of glass in the window before he was subdued. When he sat down at last, he said quietly that he was dying of a disease of the heart, and that he wished to tell them his story before the end.

In the central part of the great North American continent there lies an arid and repulsive desert, which for many a long year served as a barrier against the advance of civilisation. It is a region of desolation and silence, where nothing moves but the slow wheel of a vulture and nothing grows but a few dusty clumps of bitter bush. The traveller who strays into it may march for days without seeing a tree, a river or a living soul.

On the fourth of May 1847, at the foot of a lonely and weather-beaten rock, a man and a small girl sat together in the glare of the afternoon sun. The man was gaunt and ragged, with a face worn by hunger and a beard grey with dust, and he seemed to be about fifty years of age. His name, as they would learn, was John Ferrier, and in his arms lay a child of about five years old, with a pale and drooping face.

Ferrier's mules had perished one by one in the heat, and now his flask was empty and his last scrap of food was long since gone. A party of travellers had started out with him from the banks of the Missouri, but the plain had taken them all, and the bones of their animals lay bleaching on the track behind. He alone of that company remained alive, together with the little girl, whom he held to his breast.

The child, whose name was Lucy, opened her eyes and asked in a small, hoarse voice where her mother and father had gone, and when they would come to fetch her. Ferrier could scarcely answer, for the questions cut him to the heart, and he told her softly that they had gone ahead and that he would take care of her. He promised that she should want for nothing while he had breath in his body.

In the bottom of his flask there remained a single mouthful of water, which he had been keeping for the last extremity, and he held it to the child's parched lips. She drank it eagerly, and when she asked whether he would not have any too, he told her gently that he was not thirsty. It was the lie of a good man, and it was the last act of kindness that he supposed he would ever perform.

Lucy nestled against his shoulder and fell asleep, her small hand curled in the front of his tattered coat, and the sun began to sink in a blaze of red behind the distant hills. Ferrier, too weak now to rise from the ground, resigned himself to the thought that neither of them would see another day. He closed his eyes, and prayed in a whisper that the child at least might be spared.

When he opened his eyes again, something strange caught his attention at the very edge of the eastern horizon, where the plain ran into the sky. It was a small cloud of dust, white and faint, that seemed at first no more than a trick of the failing light. But as he watched, it grew larger and more distinct, until he could no longer doubt that something was moving towards him.

Gradually the cloud resolved itself into a long train of wagons with white canvas covers, escorted by horsemen and followed by herds of oxen and cattle. Ferrier counted the wagons until he lost count, and he realised that this was a whole people on the march, a great company of men, women and children travelling westward. He tried to shout, but his throat was too dry, and only a hoarse whisper came out.

A single horseman, however, had seen the little group beside the rock, and he came galloping across the sand and sprang down from his saddle. He gave the two travellers water from a leather flask, a few drops at a time, and told them to drink slowly, lest the sudden draught should kill them. Then he lifted the child gently in his arms, and led his horse back towards the wagons with Ferrier stumbling at his side.

The man in command of the train was an elder with a stern, hard face and a plain brown coat, and he looked down at the rescued pair with eyes that gave nothing away. He told them that his people were Saints, the chosen followers of a prophet, and that they were journeying to a promised land in the west. He would carry them with him, he said, but only on the condition that they should accept the faith that he held.

Ferrier, too exhausted to argue and too grateful to refuse, said that he would believe anything the elder liked if it would save the child. The old man gave him a long and searching look, nodded coldly and replied that the two of them might ride in the wagons, but that they would be watched. It was not a warm welcome, but to a man who had been waiting to die, it was the sweetest sound in the world.

A kind-hearted woman of the party took Lucy into her wagon and wrapped her in warm blankets, and fed her with milk and bread until her strength returned. Day by day Ferrier, too, grew stronger under the plain food and the regular rest, and the colour came slowly back into his face. As for the child, she was soon laughing again, and she became the pet of the whole train.

For weeks the long procession crawled on, fording wide and treacherous rivers, hauling the wagons up steep and stony passes and enduring heat by day and bitter cold by night. Yet the Saints were a people of extraordinary courage and discipline, and they laboured side by side without complaint, for they believed that a great reward was waiting at the journey's end. Ferrier, who had known what it was to be alone in the wilderness, admired them more than he cared to say.

It soon became clear that Ferrier was a better hunter than most of the company, for he had learned the ways of the wild country in many years of wandering. He rode far ahead of the train to find game and to search for water, and more than once his skill saved the Saints from hunger. In this way, by degrees, the suspicious elders began to treat him with respect, in spite of the fact that he was a stranger.

At last, one bright morning, the train came over a ridge and saw below it a broad green valley, with a great salt lake gleaming in the distance. The Prophet, Brigham Young, rode to the front of the line and declared that this was the place, the promised land that had been shown to him in a dream. A shout of joy went up from the weary travellers, and many of them fell upon their knees.

The Prophet began at once to plan a city, which he marked out in squares by driving sticks into the ground, and the work of building began without delay. Each family received a piece of land in proportion to its standing in the church, so that the elders had the finest fields and the humblest members took what remained. It was a stern but orderly system, and few people dared to question it.

Ferrier, who had proved himself on the road, was given a generous plot at the edge of the valley, and he built a log house on it with his own hands. It was a plain place, but it was snug and strong, with a stout door and a wide fireplace, and when it was finished he and Lucy sat down on its threshold and looked out over their new home. For the first time in years he felt that he had a place in the world.

Ferrier was clever with the soil and tireless in his labour, and his fields soon grew rich and green under his care. He planted orchards and grain, he bred fine horses and fat cattle, and he sold what he did not need to the travellers who passed through the valley. Within a few years, he had become one of the most prosperous farmers in the whole community.

There was one thing, however, that the Saints could not forgive him, and it was that he refused to take a wife. They taught that a man ought to have several, and the elders urged him again and again to follow the custom, but he would not do so. He never explained his reasons, but his neighbours began to whisper, and in the whispers there was already a hint of danger.

Meanwhile Lucy grew up happy and strong on the farm, with the sun, the air and the open land as her companions, and with her adopted father to guide her. She had the free and brave spirit of a child who has seen the worst of the world and survived it, and she was as much at home on a horse as in the kitchen. Ferrier loved her as dearly as if she had been his own flesh and blood, and she returned his love with all her heart.

The years rolled by, and thirteen of them had passed since the day that Ferrier had found a place in the valley, and Lucy, now nearly eighteen, had grown into a tall and graceful young woman. She had a clear brown skin, a ready smile and a pair of bright eyes that seemed to hold the sunshine of the country she had grown up in. There was not a farmhouse in all the valley that did not know her as the Flower of Utah.

One morning in the month of May 1860, Lucy mounted her favourite horse, a swift and nervous bay, and rode into the town to buy things for the farm. As she was making her way along the dusty street, she heard a distant roar like the sound of a gathering storm. It was a vast herd of half-wild cattle, driven by rough-looking riders, which was pouring down the road from the plains.

The herd came on in a wild, confused mass of tossing horns and rolling eyes, and the dust rose in a thick cloud that hid the ground. Lucy's horse, terrified by the noise, plunged forward into the very heart of the herd, and she soon found that she could neither stop nor turn it. Wedged among the great beasts, jostled on every side, she felt her strength failing and gave herself up for lost.

At that moment a young horseman, who had been watching the herd from the roadside, dashed into the midst of it on a strong grey horse and caught her bridle in his hand. With wonderful skill and coolness he forced his way through the press of cattle, and pulled her horse after him until they were out of danger. Not until they had reached the side of the road did Lucy realise that her heart was beating wildly, and that she was safe.

The stranger took off his hat, and she saw that he was a tall, sun-browned young man of about twenty-five, with a frank face and a steady grey eye. He said that he hoped she was not hurt, and when she thanked him, he gave his name as Jefferson Hope. He was a hunter and a miner, he added, lately come from the silver mines of Nevada, and she felt that she had never met so modest a man.

When she told her father about the adventure that evening, Ferrier took the young man by both hands and thanked him with a trembling voice. He said that he owed him more than he could ever repay, since Lucy was all he had in the world, and he begged him to come and stay at the farm as long as he pleased. Hope, who had liked the old man at first sight, gladly accepted the invitation.

He stayed for week after week, and as the days passed, he and Lucy took long rides together and walked in the orchard in the cool of the evening. They talked of the wide country he had seen, of the mountains and the mining camps and the long trails across the desert, and she listened as if she could never hear enough. Before the summer had half run its course, it was clear to both of them that they had fallen deeply in love.

One night, after Lucy had gone to bed, Hope sat down by the fire opposite the old man and told him plainly that he loved his daughter, and that he wished to marry her. Ferrier's face lit up with pleasure, for he could think of no one he would sooner trust with her happiness. But he sighed at once, and said that the Saints would never allow the daughter of so prosperous a household to marry an outsider like Hope.

After long thought, Ferrier said that he would give his consent on one condition: that Hope should return to Nevada, earn enough to establish a home and come back for Lucy within two months. They would say nothing to any person in the valley, he said, and when Hope returned, the three of them would quietly leave Utah together and seek somewhere that they might be free. He held out his rough, weathered hand, and Hope, with a solemn look, grasped it firmly and held it a long moment.

Hope promised to return before the time was out, and swore that no power on earth should keep him from his word. Early the next morning he saddled his horse, and Lucy, who had been crying quietly all night, came out to the gate to say goodbye. She stood and waved until he was only a small dark speck on the white road, and then she turned slowly back to the house with her face wet with tears.

Week after week went by, and no word came from Nevada, and Lucy, who had never lost her cheerfulness in the worst of times, grew pale and silent. Ferrier saw the change in her and said nothing, but he threw himself into his work with such fury that he was in the fields from dawn until dark. It was easier, he found, to tire his body than to quiet his mind.

One evening, as the sun was sinking behind the hills and the air was loud with the sound of the crickets, Ferrier looked up and saw a solitary rider coming slowly up the road. He knew the grim, heavy face before the horse had reached the gate, for the visitor was none other than Brigham Young himself, the Prophet of the Saints. With a heavy heart he went out to welcome him, and asked him to come in and rest.

The Prophet seated himself at the table with a stiff and solemn air, and for a long time he sat in silence, as if he were weighing his words. At last he said, in a low and measured voice, that the church had treated Ferrier well, and that it had saved him from death in the desert. He added, however, that Ferrier had never truly accepted the faith, and that this had given many people reason for complaint.

The Prophet went on to say that Lucy had reached an age at which she ought to be married, and that he had considered the matter carefully. There were two young men among the elders' sons, he said, who were worthy of her, one the son of Elder Stangerson and the other the son of Elder Drebber, and she must choose between them. It was the custom of the church, he told Ferrier, and the church expected that custom to be kept.

Ferrier, with his head bowed, pleaded that Lucy was still very young, that she had not been brought up in the ways of the Saints, and that he needed more time to prepare her. The Prophet listened without a flicker of expression, and then he gave Ferrier thirty days in which to make her ready. He warned him, as he rose from the table, that those who set themselves against the church had often come to a bad end.

The Prophet went out without another word, and Ferrier stood in the doorway listening to the clatter of the horse's hoofs as it died away in the darkness. His knees were trembling, and his face was wet with sweat, for he knew well what the Prophet's warning meant. There were men in the valley, he remembered, who had defied the elders and had afterwards vanished, and no one dared to ask where they had gone.

That night he lay awake for hours, turning over every plan that he could think of, and above all the thought of flight, over the mountains, with Lucy. Yet the passes out of the valley were watched by sentinels, who stopped every traveller, and a man who left without leave was hunted down as an enemy. Without a guide who knew the hidden paths, he realised, they could not hope to escape, and the only man who could lead them was far away in Nevada.

At breakfast he told Lucy everything the Prophet had said, and watched the colour drain from her cheeks as she listened. But she was a brave girl, and when he had finished, she took his rough hand in both of hers and said steadily that she would rather die than marry either of those men. Ferrier kissed her on the forehead, and he felt that this was the first moment of hope that he had known since the Prophet's visit.

Ferrier now sought out a trusted traveller, a man who was passing through the valley on his way to Nevada, and who was no friend to the church. In secret, he gave him a folded letter, which begged Hope to return with all speed, since Lucy was in the greatest danger and there was not a day to lose. He paid the man more than the journey was worth, and watched him ride off into the dust of the morning.

Within a few days the two young men, Stangerson and Drebber, called on Ferrier together, each of them arrogant, and each assured that the girl could not refuse him. They had scarcely entered the room before they began to quarrel over which of them had the better right to Lucy, until their voices rose into a shout. Ferrier, who could bear it no longer, seized them by their collars and threw them both out of his house, and the door shut behind them with a crash.

Ferrier marked the days one by one on the wall of his kitchen, and each night he told Lucy, in a voice that he tried to keep cheerful, to keep up her courage. In spite of his efforts, the strain began to show on his face, and he started at every sound, whether it was a footstep on the road or the creak of a board in the house. The thirty days that the Prophet had given him seemed to be running through his fingers like sand.

A few mornings after the Prophet's visit, he awoke to find a small square of paper pinned to the counterpane of his bed, directly above his chest. On it was written in a clear hand the figure twenty-six, and Ferrier, who had bolted every door and window before he went to bed, stared at it in horror. Who had been in his room, he wondered, and how had the intruder come and gone without making a sound?

On the next day there was another number, and on the next another, and they grew smaller with every morning that passed. Sometimes it was chalked on the wall of the barn, sometimes painted on the gate, sometimes laid in small stones on the path, and always in a place that he would be sure to find. No one in the valley ever saw the hand that made these marks, and that, to Ferrier, was the worst thing about them.

His neighbours, who had been friendly for years, now crossed the road to avoid meeting him, and when he spoke to them, they looked away without answering. It seemed to Ferrier that every window in the valley held a watching face, and that every man he met knew what was coming. He felt himself shut in on every side, as an animal feels when the hunters begin to close their ring.

Night after night he sat up by the open window, with a loaded rifle across his knees, determined to sell his life dearly if anyone should try to enter the house. Nothing ever disturbed him but the wind in the orchard and the barking of a distant dog, yet each morning the number on the wall was a little smaller than before. He began to wonder whether he was fighting an enemy that could not be seen, and whether the fight had already been lost.

When only three days remained, Lucy, who had been brave throughout, broke down at last and wept at the kitchen table with her head on her arms. No word had come from Nevada, and Ferrier did not know whether his letter had been delivered, or whether Hope had even been found. He stroked her hair and said nothing, because he had no comfort left to give.

Late on the evening before the last but one, when the house was dark and the whole valley was still, there came a faint tapping at the window. Ferrier sprang up, seized his rifle and stole softly to the door, with his heart beating so loudly that he feared it would be heard outside. He stood there for a long moment, listening, not knowing what it was that waited in the night.

A low voice whispered his name through the keyhole, and when he cautiously drew back the bolt, a tall figure slipped inside and closed the door behind him. It was Jefferson Hope, grey with dust and haggard with fatigue, who had ridden day and night over the mountains as soon as he had heard the news. Ferrier wrung his hand, and Lucy, who had come running from her bed, flung herself into his arms.

Hope said briefly that there was no time for explanations, and that they must leave the valley that very night, before the last of the days had run out. He had food and horses hidden among the trees, he told them, and he had learned the secret signs by which the sentinels in the passes could be passed without a shot. It was a desperate plan, but it was the only one they had, and Ferrier agreed to it without a word.

In a few minutes the two of them had collected all that they dared to carry, a little food, a few blankets and some water, and they packed them by the light of a single candle. Ferrier cast one last glance around the kitchen where he had spent thirteen peaceful years, at the fields and orchards that were the work of his hands. Then he blew out the flame and stepped out into the darkness, leaving the house and the rich farm behind him for ever.

At midnight the three of them stole out of the sleeping farmyard and across the dark fields, bent almost double and moving without a sound. In a thicket of trees at the far side of the orchard, Hope had hidden two horses and a mule, which stood waiting patiently with their loads already strapped on. Ferrier lifted Lucy into the saddle, wrapped her in a blanket and then mounted the second horse himself.

They rode all that night without exchanging a single word, with Hope a little ahead, leading them by lanes and field edges that no one else would be likely to use. The only sounds were the soft footsteps of the animals and the beating of their own hearts, and the stars wheeled slowly overhead as if they, too, were holding their breath. Lucy, wrapped in her blanket, never once complained, though she was shaking with cold and fear.

At the mouth of the first pass, where the road ran between two steep walls of rock, a sentinel stepped out of the shadows with his rifle held ready and called out a challenge. Hope reined in his horse, leaned forward and gave the secret answer in a low and level voice, as though it were the most ordinary thing in the world. After a moment's silence, the guard stepped aside and let them go by, and Ferrier let out a long breath.

At a second post, farther on, they were stopped again, and again Hope gave the sign that he had learned from a friend in the valley. The sentinel, a young man with a sleepy face, looked them over with some suspicion, but he could find nothing wrong in the answer, and he waved them on with a yawn. They rode forward into the darkness, and for the first time Ferrier felt that they might really win through.

As the first grey light of dawn began to creep across the sky, Hope turned his horse off the road and led the little party up into the hills, where no patrol would think to search. Behind them the valley lay quiet and distant, wrapped in morning mist, and ahead of them rose the steep, rocky mountains that stood between them and freedom. Nobody spoke, but the same thought was in every mind, that the worst of the danger was yet to come.

Hope led them next along a hidden track that wound along the face of a cliff on a ledge scarcely wide enough for a single horse. Far below them a torrent roared in the bottom of a gorge, and the animals trembled and snorted as they were led carefully forward by the bridle. One false step would have meant a fall of many hundred feet, and nobody dared to look down.

Near a third pass they heard the sound of hoofs on the road below, and Hope, with a sharp gesture, drew them quickly behind a great pile of fallen rocks. They crouched there in the dust, hardly daring to breathe, while a party of armed horsemen rode slowly past within a stone's throw of their hiding place. Lucy pressed her face into her father's shoulder, and it seemed to all of them that the silence would never end.

By nightfall, having seen no one further, they came at last to a little hollow among the tall rocks of Eagle Canyon, a hidden, grassy place where a spring trickled out of the stone. Hope kindled a very small fire in a crack between the boulders, and they ate the last of their food in silence while the stars came out above them. Lucy, worn out by the long journey, laid her head on her father's coat and was asleep in a minute.

Hope looked into the empty bags and told Ferrier gravely that they could not hope to cross the great desert on the road without a supply of meat. There was game in the mountains, he said, and with a little luck he should be able to shoot a deer or a mountain sheep in the morning and come back before nightfall. In the meantime, Ferrier was to stay in the hollow, to guard Lucy and to keep the fire low.

At the first light of day, Hope slung his rifle over his shoulder, bade Lucy a cheerful farewell and began to climb the steep slope that rose behind the hollow. Twice he turned to wave at her, and she waved back from her seat beside the spring, with her father at her side. He had promised to be home by evening, and neither of them doubted that he would keep his word.

Hope hunted all day among the crags and ravines without seeing a living thing, and it was late in the afternoon before he came upon a mountain sheep and brought it down. Cheered by his luck, he loaded the carcass upon his shoulders and started back, but the sun was low, and in the dusk, the canyons all looked alike. He took one wrong turning after another, and it was hours before he could find the path that led to the hollow.

It was far into the night when at last he reached the rocky hollow with the sheep still on his back, and he paused at the entrance, puzzled, because he could see no gleam of a fire. A strange stillness lay over the place, and when he called out the names of his friends, his voice came back to him from the cliffs without any answer. A cold fear took hold of him, and he began to run towards the spring.

In the starlight he saw that the camp had been torn apart, and the blankets and bundles lay scattered over the ground, while the earth was trampled by the hoofs of a great many horses. Beside the little spring, where he had left Lucy and her father sleeping, there rose a fresh mound of earth that had not been there that morning. He stood before it for a long time, unable to move or to think.

On the mound a piece of paper had been fixed to a stick, and in the faint light, Hope bent down and read the words, which stated that John Ferrier, formerly of Salt Lake City, had died there. There was no mark of any kind to tell him what had become of Lucy, and the horses and the mule had been driven away. The silence of the mountains seemed to press upon his head like a hand.

He dropped on his knees beside the grave and, for the first time since he had been a child, burst into tears, for he had loved the old man like a father. But grief cannot last for ever in a strong heart, and in a little while it gave way to a cold and bitter fury. He rose, wiped his eyes and swore that he would discover where they had taken Lucy, and that he would follow the guilty men to the end of the earth.

He made his way back toward the valley, travelling by night and lying hidden by day, living on what he could shoot and trusting to his skill in the wilds. On the edge of the settlement he met by chance a hunter named Cowper, an old friend, who was one of the Saints but had never quite forgiven the church for its ways. Cowper looked around cautiously, took him into a barn and gave him bread and water.

With his voice lowered to a whisper, Cowper told him the whole story, which was that a party of the elders' men had followed the fugitives and found them in the canyon. They had killed the old man where he stood, he said, and carried Lucy back to the town, where nobody had dared to speak a word of protest. Hope listened in silence, and his face grew harder and whiter with every sentence.

Lucy had been given no choice, Cowper said, for she was forced to marry Drebber, the very man who had come to the farm to quarrel with his rival over her hand. Drebber, who was already rich, took possession of Ferrier's farm and cattle in the name of the church, and Lucy, who was hardly more than a girl, found herself shut up in a house full of his other wives. She had no friend left in the world to whom she could turn for help or comfort.

Lucy, who had always been so strong and merry, could not bear the shame and the sorrow, and she faded day by day like a flower that has been cut. She hardly spoke and hardly ate, and she looked out of the window at the road along which Hope had gone, as if she expected him to ride back at any moment. Within a month of that unhappy wedding she was dead, and the whole valley said that she had died of a broken heart.

On the night before the funeral, Hope, with a trapper's cap pulled down over his eyes, stole into the house where she lay, and found the women who watched beside the body sound asleep. He bent over her in the candlelight, kissed the cold forehead that he had once kissed in happiness, and drew from her finger the thin gold wedding ring. Then, with the ring in his hand, he swore a solemn oath that Drebber and Stangerson should pay for everything with their lives.

As Hope stole out through the back of the house, a guard, half asleep at the corner of the yard, nearly saw him, and only a lucky shadow saved his life. He ran for the hills, and for many weeks he lay hidden in the mountains, living upon what he could shoot and never going near a road. In the silence of the rocks he turned over his oath again and again, until it had become a part of himself.

A year later he ventured back into the valley, disguised as an old trapper, with his hair grown long and his face tanned almost black by wind and sun. He made cautious inquiries, and he learned, with a bitter pang, that Drebber and Stangerson had quarrelled with the Prophet over the spoils of Ferrier's farm and had left the settlement, taking all their money with them. His enemies had escaped him, but he swore that they should not escape for long.

He set out upon their trail, and for the next few years he followed it across the length and breadth of America, working in mines and on farms whenever he needed money, and tramping where he could not ride. The wedding ring never left his pocket, and whenever he was tired or discouraged, he took it out and looked at it, and the sight revived his resolve. It was the only thing in the world that still gave his life a meaning.

Year after year he searched one town after another, and in each one he found that the men had been seen and had only just gone. He learned the arts of the hunter in a new field, listening to gossip, watching hotel doors and studying the faces in crowds. He grew thin and rough and silent, a man with a single thought, and he never allowed himself to stop for more than a night.

At length, in the city of Cleveland, in the state of Ohio, he came round a corner and saw Drebber standing on the opposite side of the street, smoking a cigar and talking to a friend. For a moment the two men stared at each other across the traffic, and Hope saw the colour drain from the other's face. Then Drebber turned and ran, and Hope, to his lasting regret, lost him in the crowd.

Drebber, recovering from his fright, went to the law, and told a judge that a man had followed him across the continent and had threatened to take his life. Hope was arrested and brought into court, where he was warned that he must keep away from the gentleman or be locked up for good. In the end he was sent to prison for several weeks, a short term, but one that proved fatal to his plans.

When Hope was set free, he hurried to the house where Drebber had been living, only to find that it was shut and empty. The two men had gathered up all their money and sailed away for Europe, and no one in the city could tell him what ship they had taken or where they were going. It was another cruel blow, and it seemed to him that fortune itself was against him.

Hope had scarcely a dollar to his name, and he knew that he could not pay for a passage, so he got work on a ship as a deck hand. He scrubbed the planks and carried coal for the stokers, and he put up with the rough jokes of the crew as the vessel crossed the grey Atlantic. All the time, the only thing that he thought about was the day he would meet his enemies once more.

In Europe, he followed them from one capital to another, to St Petersburg, to Copenhagen and to Paris, picking up their trail in hotel registers and from the memories of porters. Each time, when he arrived at some great hotel, he learned that they had left a day or two before. Drebber had a quick instinct for danger and seemed to know that someone was after him, and a man with less determination than Hope would have given up long before.

The long chase, however, was wearing him out, and the sleepless nights, the cold, the bad food and the hardships of the road were doing their work on a body that had never been strong. He began to feel a sharp pain in his chest, and at last a doctor examined him and told him that the main vessel of his heart was weakened. He could not last long, the doctor said, and he must have rest, but Hope heard him with a calm face, for he had no time to spare.

On reaching London, Hope bought a cab and a horse with all the money he had saved, and took out a licence as a driver, for he thought that nothing was better for his purpose. A cab, he reasoned, could take a man to every corner of the great city without causing the least suspicion, and nobody ever looks closely at the driver. He soon knew the streets as well as any man in England, and he waited, with the patience of long habit, for his luck to turn.

One day, as he sat on his box in a busy street, he caught sight of two men on the pavement, and his heart leaped, for they were Drebber and Stangerson. Walking his horse behind them, he followed until they came to a respectable house in Torquay Terrace, Camberwell, which proved to be a boarding house kept by a widow. He took careful note of the address, and then he drove slowly away, with his mind already full of plans.

For weeks after this, he followed the two men wherever they went, hoping for a chance to catch Drebber by himself. But they had become cautious in their old age, and they were never apart, whether by day or by night, and Hope could find no opening. He waited patiently, however, like a hunter beside a deer trail, for he knew that sooner or later they would make a mistake.

The chance came on the last night, when Drebber, after a violent quarrel in the house, left in a drunken rage and drove to Euston station. Hope, who had followed him all the way, saw him go into a bar and stay there until he came out reeling and unsteady, without his friend. Quick as thought, Hope drew his cab up beside him, and offered him a ride in a friendly voice.

Hope drove his passenger to the empty house in Brixton Road, which he had noticed some days before and for which he had managed to obtain a key. Helping the half-conscious man down from the cab, he led him up the garden path and into the front room, and closed the door behind him. The place was dark and silent, and the only sound was Drebber's heavy breathing.

Hope lit a stump of candle that he had brought with him and set it on the mantelpiece, and in its flicker the drunken man seemed to wake. Then Hope told him who he was, and who it was that he had come for, and he asked him whether he remembered a girl called Lucy Ferrier. He held the little ring before his eyes, and Drebber's face went the colour of ashes.

From his pocket Hope took out a small box, which held two pills, and he explained quietly that one was harmless and the other full of poison. Drebber should choose one of them and take it, he said, while Hope would swallow the other, and so the question of who should live would be decided by chance alone. It was a fairer chance, said Hope, than the one that Drebber had given to Lucy.

Drebber, shaking with fear, begged for mercy, but when Hope refused to hear him, he picked up a pill and put it in his mouth. It was the poisoned one, and within a minute he fell to the floor, dead. In the heat of the moment Hope's nose began to bleed, and, dipping his finger in the blood, he wrote RACHE upon the wall, to set the police on a false scent.

He drove away to a distance, and it was then that he put his hand in his pocket and found that Lucy's ring was gone, having dropped from him when he stooped over the body. Alarmed lest it should be discovered, he turned the cab back to Brixton Road and got down at the gate, only to find a constable standing there with his lantern. Hope acted the part of a drunkard so well that the man helped him to the corner and let him go.

On the following night Hope found Stangerson at his hotel, and he waited until the house was quiet and climbed a ladder that lay in the yard to a window on the second floor. Stangerson, awake, would not take either pill, and sprang at him with a knife, so that Hope was forced to stab him in his own defence. Then, dipping a finger in the blood, he wrote RACHE a second time upon the wall.

When Hope had reached the end of his story, he leaned back in his chair and said quietly that his work was done, and that he had nothing further to confess. It was fortunate, he added, that he had been able to finish, for he could not tell how many hours were left to him. As for the old woman who had called for the ring, she had been a loyal friend of his, a gifted actor in disguise, and she had restored the ring to him that very evening.

He declared that he felt no shame for what he had done, since he had punished two guilty men and had kept the promise he made beside Lucy's body. Gregson and Lestrade, who had listened to the whole account with unusual attention, rose and took him gently by the arms. He went with them without any struggle, and the door of the sitting room closed behind the three men.

On the following day the prisoner was brought before the magistrates, and the room was crowded with people eager to hear the story of the Brixton murders. Hope told it again in the same calm and steady voice, and he made no attempt to excuse himself or to deny any part of it. The magistrates remanded him to prison, and announced that he would be tried at the assizes on the following day.

But on the morning before the trial the warder, opening the door of the cell, found the prisoner lying upon his bed, quite dead. His face wore a placid and peaceful expression, and there was a smile upon his lips, as though he had been able to look back in his last moments upon a useful life and a duty well done. It was the end of a long pursuit, and no one in the prison could recall a more quiet death.

The doctor who examined the body reported that the great blood vessel of the heart had burst during the night, from a disease of long standing which Hope himself had known about. Watson, who had felt the man's pulse on the evening of his arrest, was not surprised in the least, and said as much to Holmes. It seemed that the hand of fate had spared the law the trouble of any further judgement.

Holmes, sitting by the fire with his pipe, explained to Watson how he had come at the truth, and he did so in his usual quiet and detached way. Most people, he said, if you describe to them a train of events, can tell you what the result will be, but few can take the result and work out for themselves the steps that led up to it. This power, which he called reasoning backward or analytically, was the whole secret of his trade.

The wedding ring had told him that there was a woman in the case, he said, and the footprints and the wheel marks had told him of a tall man who came in a cab. The pills had shown a cruel and patient revenge, and the telegram from Cleveland, which named Jefferson Hope, had given him the last link in the chain. After that it was a matter of finding a particular cab among the thousands in London, and of luring its driver to the one place where he could be taken.

On the next morning the newspapers broke into praise for Gregson and Lestrade, who, according to the reports, had followed the clues with the greatest skill and had arrested the murderer in the nick of time. Nobody mentioned the name of Sherlock Holmes, and nobody mentioned the little room in Baker Street where the thing had really been done. Watson read the account aloud with growing indignation, while Holmes sat listening with an air of weary amusement.

Holmes only laughed, and said that this was exactly what he had expected, since he was an unofficial person and would never be thanked for his work. He quoted a verse about a miser in Rome, who hears the people hiss at him but applauds himself at home, as he counts the coins in his chest. Watson answered firmly that the public must know the facts, and that he himself would write them down and publish them, whatever the police might say.

That very night, Watson sat down at the table under the lamp, with his pen and a pile of paper, and set about the story of the strange case from the beginning. Holmes, lying in his armchair with his violin across his knee, said that the whole affair was a study in scarlet, for there was the scarlet thread of murder running through the colourless skein of life. Outside, the lamps of Baker Street were lighting one by one, and so began a partnership that the world would never forget.
